4  Assessment of Volume Status in the CCU
3
CVP can accurately predict fluid responsiveness in only 56% of cases, and these types of static 
measures do not predict whether fluid loading will result in an increase in cardiac output. In addi-
tion, fluid has to be given before the response to fluid challenge can be evaluated in an emergency 
situation (which is potentially hazardous).
Dynamic parameters predict the response to fluid loading without having to give a fluid chal-
lenge, so they may avoid the potential hazards of a fluid challenge.
  6.	What are the static measures of fluid responsiveness?
CVP
Required equipment: Central venous line
Provides estimate of right atrial pressure. It is ideally measured at the junction of the SVC and the 
right atrium.
Factors affecting: Blood volume, vascular tone, right ventricular function and compliance, tricus-
pid valve disease, cardiac rhythm, intrathoracic pressure (respiratory efforts and peak end- 
expiratory pressure [PEEP])
Patient position—Normal: 1–8 cm of water
Target (during sepsis): 8–12 cm of water
Limitations: The ability of any CVP value to accurately predict volume responsiveness is about 56%. 
In patients with intact vascular tone, a decrease in CVP is a relatively late sign of intravascular 
volume depletion.
PAOP
Required equipment: Central access with an 8.5F introducer catheter to insert the pulmonary artery 
catheter.
Normal value: 4–12 cm of water.
Significance: Also known as pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP), it approximates left atrial 
pressure and left ventricular end-diastolic pressure. It is used as a surrogate for left ventricular 
end-diastolic volume, assuming a linear pressure-volume relationship in the left ventricle (LV). 
For assessing volume responsiveness, a single PAOP reading has a positive predictive value in 
the range of 50%.
GEDVI (Global End Diastolic Volume Index)
Required equipment: Central venous catheter and thermistor-tipped femoral arterial line to per-
form transpulmonary thermodilution, which is known as a pulse contour cardiac output 
(PiCCO) system. PiCCO can estimate cardiac output, preload and degree of pulmonary 
oedema.
Normal value: 680–800 mL/m2
Importance: It is a moderate predictor of volume responsiveness. When it is utilized with stroke 
volume variation (SVV) obtained from the PiCCO system, it may improve the ability to detect 
volume responsiveness.
LVEDA
Required equipment: Transoesophageal echocardiography
An LVEDA of less than 10 cm2 or an LVEDA index (LVEDA/BSA) of less than 5.5 cm2/m2 indicates 
significant hypovolaemia.
LVEDA alone is a poor predictor of volume responsiveness. In the absence of baseline echocardio-
graphic data about absolute value of LVEDA, the values are difficult to interpret.
Another qualitative sign that suggests severe hypovolaemia is the “kissing papillary muscle sign” 
where opposing papillary muscles come in contact with each other at end systole.
  7.	 What are the principles of dynamic variation of fluid responsiveness?
The principles of dynamic variables are explained next.
BK-TandF-SIKDAR_9781032455174-220973-Eresource_4.indd   3
15/02/23   3:01 PM
Swarup Paul and Sunandan Sikdar
4
Transmural pressure is the pressure difference between inside the aorta and outside (pleural). 
During inspiration in a mechanically ventilated (positive pressure ventilation) patient, afterload to 
the LV decreases due to a decrease in transmural pressure and preload to the LV increases due to 
squeezing of pulmonary capillary blood to the left side of the heart. This leads to an increase in LV 
output during inspiration and increased systolic pressure, increased pulse pressure and increased 
stroke volume.
During inspiration in a mechanically ventilated patient with positive pressure ventilation, the 
right ventricle preload decreases due to a decrease in venous return (decrease preload due to 
decreased IVC – intrathoracic gradient) and afterload increases due to inflation of the lung, which 
results in decreased right ventricle output. This leads to a decrease in systolic pressure, pulse pres-
sure and stroke volume of the right ventricle, which is reflected as a reduction of stroke volume of the 
LV during expiration due to transit time from the right to the left side of heart.
Hence, in mechanically ventilated patients, stroke volume decreases at the end of expiration and increases 
at the end of inspiration.
These changes will result in SVV, systolic pressure variation (SPV) and PPV with the respira-
tory cycle. These parameters increase during inspiration and decrease during expiration and are 
referred to as dynamic indicators of preload responsiveness.
  8.	What are the prerequisites to assess volume responsiveness by the markers SVV, SPV and 
PPV?
There are three preconditions:
a.	 Normal sinus rhythm
b.	 Totally mechanically ventilated with no spontaneous breathing attempts
c.	 Tidal volume adequate, i.e., 8–10 mL/kg
  9.	 What are the conditions where dynamic measures can lead to pitfalls?
There are three conditions:
1.	 Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)
2.	 Intra-abdominal hypertension
3.	 Right heart failure
The dynamic response variables are not useful in ARDS, where small tidal volume coupled with 
stiff lungs render the measurement thresholds impracticable.

PPV
PPV is calculated as the difference between the maximum and minimum pulse pressure during a respiratory 
cycle divided by the average of the two values. This automated measurement is performed by the major-
ity of bedside monitors.

A PPV or stroke volume variation of more than 10%–12% predicts volume responsiveness with high 
sensitivity and specificity.
Fluid Responders and Non-Responders
If stroke volume or cardiac output increases by more than 15% with a fluid challenge or in response 
to a passive leg-raise (PLR) test, then the patient is a fluid responder.
If stroke volume or cardiac output increases by 10%–15% along with evidence of end-organ hypo-
perfusion, the patient is fluid responsive and may benefit from a fluid bolus.
If stroke volume or cardiac output increases by less than 10%, then the patient is not a fluid 
responder.

4  Assessment of Volume Status in the CCU

11.	What is the role of ScvO2 (central venous oxygen saturation) monitoring?
ScvO2 is used as a surrogate of true SvO2 (mixed venous oxygen saturation). It is measured in the 
SVC through an ordinary central venous catheter (whereas a pulmonary artery catheter is required 
to measure SvO2). It reflects the balance between oxygen delivery (DO2) and demand (VO2). SvO2 > 
ScvO2, as SvO2 contains blood from both the IVC and SVC, whereas ScvO2 contains predominantly 
blood from the SVC (which is more desaturated than IVC blood).
An SvO2 below 65% indicates low oxygen delivery. A value below 60% implies that there is a 
serious risk of tissue hypoxia and immediate measures are needed. A low SvO2 (<40%) indicates 
a critical oxygen supply-demand imbalance. High SvO2 (>80%) indicates either the demand has 
declined or the oxygen supply has increased, or there is poor utilization of oxygen by the cells.
In septic shock, the goal of early resuscitation, within 6 hr, is to keep SvO2 greater than 65%.
12.	What is the PLR test?
Requirements for mechanical ventilation and sedation are major limitations of the dynamic tech-
niques of haemodynamic monitoring in intensive care. PLR is used to determine volume respon-
siveness in spontaneously breathing patients. There is a gravitational transfer of blood from the legs to 
the intrathoracic cavity with resultant increases in PCWP and LV preload during PLR. PLR is best 
performed by elevating the lower limbs to 45 degrees and lowering the patient into the supine posi-
tion from a 45-degree semi-recumbent position simultaneously (Figure 4.2). This causes an increase 
of cardiac preload from the shift of venous blood from the legs as well as the abdominal compartment 
(nearly 500 mL autotransfusion). If haemodynamics improve after PLR, additional volume may be 
indicated. If haemodynamics do not improve after PLR, it can be quickly reversed by lowering the 
legs. This is an advantage over the fluid bolus technique, where the bolus cannot be quickly removed.
13.	What is the significance of the fluid challenge in the intensive care unit (ICU) setting?
Determination of volume status (i.e., position of the patient on the Frank-Starling curve) in the ICU is 
very difficult but is important to optimize haemodynamics. A time-honoured test is to give a fluid bolus 
(100–200 mL as per left ventricular ejection fraction [LVEF]) and observe for a change in haemodynam-
ics. If there is an increase in blood pressure or cardiac output after a bolus, then the patient is likely on 
the ascending portion of the Frank-Starling curve, and further fluid boluses may be given to improve 
haemodynamics. If a fluid bolus produces a minimal effect, then it is likely that the patient is near the top 
of the Frank-Starling curve. If there is deterioration in the blood pressure or cardiac output after a fluid 
bolus, then the patient may be volume overloaded on the flat/descending portion of the curve.
14.	How do you assess the IVC for fluid responsiveness?
The IVC is measured at 1.7 cm from the IVC–right atrium (RA) junction, with an echocardiography 
probe of 2–4 MHz, from the subxiphoid area (the marker dot pointing to the sternal notch). The 
following measurements suggest a spontaneously breathing patient is likely to be fluid responsive:
a.	 IVC measurement <2.1 cm in diameter along with IVC collapse >50% with each breath
Or
b.	 IVC collapsibility >12%

15.	How do you measure cardiac output?
Transoesophageal Doppler
Cardiac output can be measured with the transoesophageal Doppler. It is based on measuring the 
velocity of blood flow through the descending aorta. In this technique, a transducer is placed into 
the oesophagus and rotation of the probe is done to achieve an optimal signal. Blood flow velocity is 
measured by Doppler. Stroke volume (SV) is derived from multiplication of a velocity time integral 
(VTI) with aortic cross-sectional area. When SV is calculated, the cardiac output (CO) is determined 
(CO = heart rate × SV).
Transpulmonary Thermodilution
Transpulmonary thermodilution measures CO by detecting a cold bolus saline within the periph-
eral arterial system. The cold saline bolus is administered through a central venous catheter and 
detected by a thermistor-tipped arterial catheter, which is placed into the radial, axillary or femoral 
artery. CO is calculated by the Stewart-Hamilton equation similar to the pulmonary artery thermo-
dilution technique.
Partial Carbon Dioxide Rebreathing
This depends upon the modified Fick principle to calculate CO. The Fick equation is based on the 
belief that oxygen uptake from the lung is completely transferred into the bloodstream. For this 
reason, CO is calculated as a ratio between oxygen consumption and the arteriovenous difference in 
oxygen content. The Fick principle is applied to CO2 instead of oxygen in the partial CO2 rebreathing 
technique.

5  Thoracic Ultrasound
Abhradip Das and Sunandan Sikdar
  1.	What is the role of thoracic ultrasound sonography (USG) in the cardiac care unit (CCU)?
Air in the lung was once considered the worst enemy of ultrasound, as it creates false images (arte­
facts). However, typical artefacts and some real images produced by the interaction of the ultrasound 
beam with the air-fluid interface may help to make an early diagnosis in certain cases. Many bed­
side real-time protocols (the bedside lung ultrasound in emergency [BLUE] protocol for the immedi­
ate diagnosis of acute respiratory failure and the fluid administration limited by lung sonography 
[FALLS] protocol) are in clinical use now. Recent studies have also demonstrated its high sensitivity 
and specificity in the diagnosis of heart failure, pneumonia, pneumothorax, pulmonary embolism 
and pleural effusion. Published performance of lung ultrasounds in critically ill patients compared 
with CT scanning are given in Table 5.1.
  2.	What are the types of tools used for thoracic USG?
A linear probe (higher frequency) is used for superficial lung structures. Convex probes (lower fre­
quency) are used for deeper structures. A micro-convex probe is used for various protocols.
There are various methods of examination. Usually, each lung is divided into three spaces on each 
side. Total six BLUE points are used for protocols (three on each side) (Figure 5.1).
  3.	What is the pleural sliding sign?
The pleura, made of parietal and visceral layers, is seen on-screen as a thick white line, which moves 
with each respiration. This is called the pleural sliding sign (Figure 5.2a). The bat sign: The ribs on both 
sides and the pleural line in between outline a silhouette which is reminiscent of a bat. This allows 
confident recognition of the pleural line in all circumstances, even in patients with acute dyspnoea, 
patients who are agitated and even in bariatric patients.

  4.	What is the seashore sign?
This is a dynamic sign seen in M-mode. The “sea” is described as straight horizontal lines produced 
by motionless skin, tissue and muscles (real image); and the “shore” is displayed as a granular 
appearance produced by moving lung (false image). This signifies a normal lung segment in sono­
logical studies.
  5.	What is the A line?
The A line is a “reverberation” artefact. It is a repetition of the pleural line (white horizontal line), 
indicating air in the lung. When the ultrasound beam traverses through skin, intercostal muscles, 
neurovascular bundles and pleura, it produces real images. When it reaches the pleura, it bounces 
back to the probe and appears as horizontal lines (A line), which are equidistant from the pleural 
line (Figure 5.2a). An A line with pleural sliding signifies a normal lung.
  6.	What are B lines?
B lines are vertical white thick lines which start from the pleura, traverse throughout and abolish 
the A line. It is also known as the “lung comet” or “lung rocket” (Figure 5.2b). When interlobular 
septa are enlarged by oedema, the ultrasound waves, while penetrating the lung, suddenly change

with preserved ejection fraction and in cases where the chest X-ray is suboptimal, or brain natri­
uretic peptide (BNP) is not available. It may also differentiate pulmonary oedema from pneumonia 
in an acutely ill patient.
  7.	 What are Z lines?
Z lines are vertical lines. Unlike B lines, Z lines don’t traverse through the screen and don’t abolish 
A lines. They are of normal variant (Figure 5.2c).
  8.	What are E lines?
These are vertical lines. They originate from above (superficial to) the pleural line (B lines originate 
from the pleura), i.e., tissue, muscle and skin. These lines are seen in subcutaneous emphysema. As 
air is a bad conductor of sound, air in the subcutaneous spaces erases all other architectural images 
with E lines (emphysema lines) (Figure 5.2d).

  9.	 What are the sonological findings in the case of consolidation (pneumonia)?
Bedside thoracic ultrasound is useful in diagnosing consolidation. The following signs are usually 
seen:
a.	 Shred sign: At the initial phase of lung consolidation, it appears as patchy B lines. Usually, it is 
associated with an irregular pleural line, and the B lines originate from various levels of the 
pleura, unlike the typical wet lung profile, where B lines originate from the smooth pleural line 
(Figure 5.3a).
b.	 Tissue-like sign: As the infective process progresses, more and more lung parenchyma get 
involved. It looks like a solid tissue (commonly as echogenic as the liver). It is pathologically 
denoted as “hepatization“ of parenchyma of the lung (Figure 5.3b).
c.	 Air bronchogram: Movement of air through terminal bronchioles in a consolidated lung paren-
chyma is well displayed by ultrasound on-screen as moving (in and out) white dots along with 
respiration. This is called a dynamic air bronchogram (Figure 5.3b). It signifies true consolida-
tion (pneumonia). A static air bronchogram may be seen in three conditions: atelectasis, the 
initial phase of collapse due to blocking of the airway and air trapping.
10.	What are the sonological findings in pleural effusion?
Bedside ultrasound is a very good tool to pick up a pleural effusion in no time with very high sensi-
tivity and specificity. It appears as an anechoic (black) area between the parietal and visceral pleura. 
It is picked up earliest at the most dependent part of the pleural cavity as per the patient’s position 
and posture. The size of the effusion changes as the position changes.

The following radiological signs are seen in pleural effusion:
a.	 Jellyfish sign: It is the freely moving collapsed lung with the rhythm of respiration within free 
fluid (Figure 5.4a). Usually, it is seen in large effusions.
b.	 Quad sign: An area of effusion is bounded by the shadow of the adjacent ribs on both sides, by the 
parietal pleura above and the visceral pleura + lung at the bottom. This is a static sign.
c.	 Sinusoid sign: It is a dynamic sign seen on M-mode. With inspiration, the visceral pleura moves 
towards the parietal pleura. It is seen in small effusions (Figure 5.4b).
d.	 Plankton sign: Floating cellular debris in fluid appears as an internal echo. The debris gets agi­
tated with respiration or cardiac pulsation. It is a real-time dynamic shadow. It signifies the 
exudative nature of the pleural fluid or a haemothorax.
11.	How does ultrasound help to determine the aetiology of a pleural effusion?
An anechoic appearance usually suggests transudative effusion. Transudative effusion is usually 
seen on both sides.
Fibrotic septa, loculations and echogenic fluid are commonly seen in exudative effusions. An 
inflammatory process causes the high protein and cellular content of pleural fluid, producing septa 
and echogenic fluid. A haemothorax may also show the same features.
12.	What is the role of USG in thoracentesis or placing an intercostal chest drain (ICD)?
Use of ultrasound in thoracentesis has significantly reduced iatrogenic pneumothorax, bleeding or 
injury to nearby solid organs.

A.	 Marking a safe puncture point: With a fixed position of the patient, an area of fluid with three or

13.	What are the signs elicited in a pneumothorax?
Rapid diagnosis of a pneumothorax is possible by the following features:
A.	 In a pneumothorax, there is an absence of lung sliding and the A line.
B.	 The presence of an A line, B line, lung sliding, lung pulse, consolidation and effusion eventually 
rules out pneumothorax on that segment.
C.	 Barcode sign or stratosphere sign: Horizontal straight motionless lines on M-mode are known as 
the barcode sign or stratosphere sign. This sign may be seen in a patient with pneumothorax.
D.	 Lung point: This is the point where the lung touches the chest wall during inspiration. This is 
displayed on-screen on M-mode an as alternate presence of the typical seashore sign on inspira­
tion and the barcode sign on expiration. It is one of the sure signs of pneumothorax. It is seen in 
a small pneumothorax.
14.	What does the diaphragm look like?
The diaphragm is seen on ultrasound as a whiter structure dividing the thoracic and abdominal 
cavity. It has two echogenic layers – on both sides there is a more whitish pleural and peritoneal line, 
with a lesser white muscle layer in between. Usually, the thickness of the diaphragm is 22–28 mm 
in healthy individuals and 13–19 mm in a paralysed diaphragm. Thickness less than 20 mm at the 
height of expiration indicates diaphragmatic atrophy.

6  Arterial Blood Gas
Swarup Paul and Sunandan Sikdar
  1.	 What is the relationship between the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation and the pH of our body?
Normal pH (7.35–7.45) is maintained by both the lungs and kidney. The normal pH in our body is 
the function of the ratio between bicarbonate and partial pressure of carbon dioxide (reflected in the 
Henderson-Hasselbalch equation). Bicarbonate is regulated by the kidney, and partial pressure of 
carbon dioxide is regulated by the lung.
  2.	What are the usual sites to draw arterial blood?
In order of preference, the sites are radial artery, femoral artery and brachial artery. In patients of severe 
burns, those with bleeding disorders, very frail and elderly patients and neonates, capillary blood gas 
can be used as surrogate (except the value of PO2). Heel in case of neonates and ear lobe in case of adults 
are the recommended sites. If the site is pre-warmed prior to sampling the PO2 results are more accurate.
  3.	What are the complications related to arterial blood sampling, and how do you prevent them?
The complications are listed here.
1.	 Arterial spasm: It may be prevented by helping the patient relax and avoiding repeated punctur-
ing of the artery.
2.	 Haematoma: This occurs especially if the patient is on anticoagulation and particularly in the 
femoral and brachial sites. It may be prevented by avoiding double puncturing of the artery and 
by applying pressure for a reasonable time immediately after blood is drawn.
3.	 Nerve damage: It is prevented by choosing an appropriate site and avoiding redirection of the needle.
4.	 Vasovagal attack: It is prevented by ensuring that the patient is in the supine position with feet 
elevated.
Other complications like fall of BP, sweating and pallor may occur in anxious patients.
  4.	What are the reasons for an inaccurate result?
1.	 Presence of air in the sample: Increases pO2 and reduces pCO2.
2.	 Venous blood rather than arterial blood: pH and pO2 are low and pCO2 is higher.
3.	 Improper quantity of heparin in the syringe or improper mixing after blood is drawn: The more 
heparin that is used, the less the pCO2 and bicarbonate; this is misinterpreted as metabolic acidosis.
4.	 Delay in specimen transportation: Decreases pH and pO2 but increases pCO2; this is misinter-
preted as respiratory acidosis.
  5.	What is the practical approach to the technique?
◾
◾Pre-heparinized syringe (1000 U/mL to fill the dead space): Heparin must lubricate the inner wall 
of syringe and then completely expelled. The blood drawn must be 20 times the dead space volume 
(the hub of syringe). This means with 2 ml syringe with 0.1 ml dead space volume, full 2 ml blood is 
required. Heparin (1000 IU/mL) contained in 0.1 ml hub now mixes with 2 ml blood to yield a final 
heparin concentration of 50 IU/mL. This is the ideal heparin concentration and is used commonly 
in India. However use of lyophilized, balanced lithium heparin has been recommended.
◾
◾Needles (20, 21, 23 and 25 gauge of different lengths): Choose a size (usually 21) that is appropriate for 
the site (Smaller gauges are more likely to lyse the specimen).
◾
◾A safety syringe with a needle cover that allows the syringe to be capped before transport, with-
out manually recapping. (This is a best practice for radial blood sampling.)
The needle should be at 45 degrees to the skin to lessen trauma.
◾
◾A bandage to cover the puncture site after collection
◾
◾A container with crushed ice for transportation of the sample to the laboratory (if the analysis is 
not done at the point of care): This keeps the sample in a more suitable state for an hour. Analysis 
should be done within 30 minutes. Pure ice should not be used as at very low temperatures, plas-
tic syringe becomes permeable to gases.

  6.	What are the types of acid-base disorders?
Simple acid base disorder: Consists of one primary disturbance and its compensatory response.
Mixed acid-base disorder: A combination of primary disturbances is present.
There are mainly two approaches
1.	 Boston approach—CO2: Bicarbonate approach
2.	 Copenhagen approach: Base deficit/excess approach
  7.	 What are the steps to interpret an arterial blood gas (ABG) reading?

PCO2 (respiratory). However, if pH is normal (7.35–45), then it may be normal or a mixed disor-

11.	What are the causes of metabolic acidosis and its treatment?
Metabolic acidosis occurs due to the addition of acids (organic or inorganic) or from the loss of bicar-
bonate (diarrhoea) or accumulation of toxic wastes (renal failure) (Table 6.3).
High AG Metabolic Acidosis
Ketoacidosis: Diabetic ketoacidosis
◾
◾Starvation
◾
◾Alcohol
◾
◾Lactic acidosis
Poisoning: Salicylates
◾
◾Ethylene glycol
◾
◾Methanol
◾
◾Renal failure
Normal AG Acidosis (Pneumonic: HARDUP)
H: Hyperalimentation
A: Acetazolamide
R: Renal tubular acidosis
D: Diarrhoea
U: Uraemia (acute)
P: Post-ventilation hypocapnia
Treatment: The first goal of therapy is to identify and correct the underlying cause. The role of alkali 
therapy in attenuating acute metabolic acidosis depends on various factors, including the underly-
ing aetiology, chronicity, severity and reversibility.
Sodium bicarbonate therapy is controversial since bicarbonate therapy itself can result in volume 
expansion, increased pCO2 generation, hypernatremia and hypocalcaemia, which all may contrib-
ute toward worsening cardiovascular depression. Bicarbonate is administered in life-threatening 
academia with a pH less than 7.1.
Two other agents which buffer H+ protons without increasing CO2 are tris-hydroxymethyl amino-
methane (THAM) and dichloroacetate (via increased oxidation of pyruvate).
12.	What are the causes of metabolic alkalosis and its treatment?
It is due to either a gain of bicarbonate or extracellular volume contraction.
Chloride Responsive or Saline Responsive (urine Cl– <20 mEq/L): 
◾
◾Gastric fluid loss
◾
◾Diuretics
◾
◾Villous adenoma
◾
◾Non-reabsorbable anion delivery

Treatment: 0.9% NaCl will reverse chloride-responsive metabolic alkalosis. Response to treatment

Chloride Unresponsive or Saline Unresponsive (urine Cl– >20 mEq/L):

Acetazolamide can be considered in cases of worsening metabolic alkalosis associated with vol-
ume overload complicated by the need for continued attempts at diuresis (nonchloride responsive).
13.	What are the causes of respiratory acidosis and its treatment?
In the case of respiratory acidosis, the primary rise in CO2 is most often due to alveolar hypoven-
tilation. The causes may be respiratory centre depression, neuromuscular disorder, upper airway 
obstruction and lung disease.
Treatment: Correction of alveolar hypoventilation and underlying cause of hypoventilation, which 
may include bronchodilators (for asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder [COPD]), 
reversal of medication/drug effects, treatment of pulmonary oedema, treatment of neuromuscular 
diseases and mechanical ventilation.
Sodium bicarbonate is not recommended in respiratory acidosis (it may cause worsening of 
hypercapnia, pulmonary oedema or metabolic alkalosis). Small doses of sodium bicarbonate can be 
considered in cases of intractable hypercapnia with severe acidosis (pH <7.1).
14.	What are the causes of respiratory alkalosis and its treatment?
In the case of respiratory alkalosis, the primary decrease in CO2 is usually due to hyperventilation, 
particularly mechanical hyperventilation, as well as pain, anxiety, sepsis, respiratory centre stimu-
lation and hypoxaemia due to any cause.
Treatment: Treat the underlying cause. Causes of hypoxia should be identified and treated. 
Acetazolamide can be used to induce a metabolic acidosis to compensate for the respiratory alkalo-
sis caused by a high altitude.

We end with three “real-world” examples.
CASE STUDY 6.1
Mr A, a 65-year-old man and known patient with COPD, presented in the emergency depart-
ment complaining of increased shortness of breath for the last 2 days along with a productive 
cough with yellow expectoration. O/E: pulse rate 112/min, BP 150/90 mmHg, SpO2 83% on 
room air, respiratory rate 30/min and the patient is restless. Chest: Bilateral rhonchi present, 
cardiovascular system unremarkable. ABG shows pH 7.32, PCO2 65 mmHg, PO2 55 mmHg, 
HCO3
– 25 mmHg, Lactate 1.2 mg/dL.
CASE STUDY 6.2
Mrs B, a 58-year-old woman, presented in the emergency department with complaints of 
sudden and severe respiratory distress with mild chest pain. She is hypertensive but non-
diabetic and is on irregular medication. ECG shows ST depression in the anterolateral leads. 
O/E: pulse rate 108/min, BP 180/110 mmHg, SpO2 91% on room air, respiratory rate 36/min and 
the patient is restless. Chest: Bilateral fine crepitations, cardiovascular exam unremarkable. 
ABG shows pH 7.39, PCO2 36 mmHg, PO2 50 mmHg, HCO3
– 22 mmHg, lactate 3.2 mg/dL.
CASE STUDY 6.3
Mr X, a 30-year-old man with no comorbidities, presented in the emergency department 
with a complaint of fever for the last 10 days along with a dry cough. O/E: Pulse rate 158/min, 
BP 84/60 mmHg, SpO2 90% on room air, respiratory rate 28/min and the patient is rest-
less and a little bit confused. Chest: Crepitations on right infra-axillary region, CVS: unre-
markable. ABG shows pH 7.34, pCO2 36 mmHg, PO2 50 mmHg, HCO3
– 22 mmHg, lactate 
6.2 mg/dL.
INTERPRETATION OF CASE STUDY 6.1
While the history is suggestive of acute exacerbation of COPD, the ABG is showing Type 2 
respiratory failure with hypoxia and respiratory acidosis. For acute respiratory compensation, 
the formula is 65 – 40/10, so that HCO3
– should be 24 + 2.5 (rule of 1, see question 15), which 
is not significantly different. That means it is a pure respiratory acidosis. Since the lactate is 
normal, tissue hypoxia has not set in, and because the diastolic BP is in the upper limit of nor-
mal, we are in the early part of sepsis/inflammatory response (vasodilation has not occurred). 
However, we can say that even if COPD is a working diagnosis, the CO2 retention was not 
that much prior to the exacerbation; otherwise, PCO2 and HCO3
– would have been higher due 
to chronic compensation (rule of 3, see question 15). Possibly he was a “pink puffer” or the 
emphysema-predominant type.

TIPS AND PITFALLS
History is very important when interpreting an ABG.
INTERPRETATION OF CASE STUDY 6.2
The history and physical exam are suggestive of diabetes with possible ischaemic heart dis-
ease, hypertension and heart failure. The ABG shows a normal pH with hypoxia and hyper-
lactataemia. That means it is a mixed acid-base disorder (but not normal, as lactate is raised). 
Since PCO2 and lactate both are low, we must have the combination of respiratory alkalosis 
with metabolic acidosis (see question 6). This is corroborated by two facts: In metabolic aci-
dosis with pH 7.39, the expected PCO2 due to compensation would be 39 mmHg (see ques-
tion 15), which is higher than the actual PCO2. Further, the respiratory rate is increased – that 
means hyperventilation is washing out CO2 and causing respiratory alkalosis. Thus, it is a 
type 1 respiratory failure along with hyperlactataemia. Again, since she is hypertensive, low 
perfusion pressure cannot be the cause of the hyperlactataemia. It may be due to any or all 
of (1) renal dysfunction associated with diabetes, (2) hyperadrenergic state (anxiety/pulmo-
nary oedema) causing peripheral vasoconstriction or (3) persistent hypoxia due to pulmonary 
oedema.
INTERPRETATION OF CASE STUDY 6.3
There is a history suggestive of sepsis and an ABG showing metabolic acidosis along with 
hyperlactataemia due to sepsis.

7  Approach to Electrolyte Abnormalities in the CCU
Swarup Paul and Sunandan Sikdar
7.1  HYPONATRAEMIA
  1.	What is the definition of hyponatraemia?
Serum Na+ concentration <135 mmol/L is defined as hyponatraemia.
  2.	What are the types of hyponatraemia?
Depending upon Duration
Acute (onset <48 hr) and Chronic (onset >48 hr)
Depending upon the Biochemical Value of Serum Na+ Concentration
Mild: 130 mmol/L to 135 mmol/L
Moderate: 125 mmol/L to 129 mmol/L
Severe: <125 mmol/L (<120 in some texts)
Depending upon symptoms (can be any biochemical degree of hyponatraemia):
Moderately symptomatic: Nausea without vomiting, confusion, headache and forgetfulness. More 
common in chronic hyponatraemia, especially with sodium <120 mmol/L.
Severely symptomatic: Neuronal injury is the primary pathophysiology of hyponatraemia symptoms 
(Figure 7.1): Vomiting, cardiorespiratory distress, abnormal and deep somnolence, seizures and 
coma. Seizures are more common in acute hyponatraemia. Fatal brain herniation, though rare, is the 
most dreaded complication of hyponatraemia.
Depending upon Osmolality
Hypo-osmolar/hypotonic (<280 mOsm/kg) hyponatraemia: The most common variety.
Iso-osmolar hyponatraemia (pseudohyponatraemia) (serum osmolality 280–290 mOsm/kg): Due to the pres-
ence of endogenous solutes: Hyperlipidaemia and hyperproteinaemia.
Hyperosmolar (hypertonic) hyponatraemia (serum osmolality >290 mOsm/kg): Hyperglycaemia and 
hypertonic infusion (mannitol, glycine).
  3.	How is the cause of hyponatraemia diagnosed?
After history and examination (looking for oedema/dehydration), check serum osmolality, urine 
osmolality and spot urine sodium and volume status (Figure 7.2).
If it is hypotonic hyponatraemia, then assess urine osmolality.
If urine osmolality ≤100 mOsm/kg (dilute urine), then consider primary polydipsia, low salt intake.

If urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg (concentrated urine), then check urine spot sodium.
If urine spot sodium concentration ≤30 mmol/L (sodium being actively reabsorbed in renal 
tubules), then check volume status.
If there is expanded extracellular fluid volume (oedematous) then consider heart failure, liver cir-
rhosis or nephrotic syndrome.
If there is reduced extracellular fluid volume, then consider diarrhoea and vomiting or third spacing 
or remote diuretics.
If urine spot sodium concentration ≥30 mmol/L (sodium reabsorption defect), then take history of 
use of diuretics or kidney disease.
Check volume status by examining for dehydration, pedal oedema and jugular venous pressure 
(JVP).
If there is reduced extracellular fluid volume, then consider vomiting, primary adrenal insuffi-
ciency, renal salt wasting or cerebral salt wasting.
If there is normal extracellular fluid volume then consider syndrome of inappropriate Anti Diuretic 
Hormone (ADH) (SIADH), secondary adrenal insufficiency or hypothyroidism.

7  Approach to Electrolyte Abnormalities in the CCU

  5.	What is the treatment of hyponatraemia?
The goal of therapy in those with less severe symptoms are to increase the serum sodium by 
6–8 mmol/L in 24 hr. In those with severe symptoms, this goal should be achieved in the initial 6 hr. 
Thereafter, the rise should be slow and care taken to avoid neurologic injury.
Treatment of hyponatraemia depends upon:
◾
◾Severity
◾
◾Duration
◾
◾Symptoms
Acute hyponatraemia, even with mild symptoms, is an emergency, as cerebral oedema may occur. 
Three percent NaCl can be started immediately via a peripheral vein; central venous access may be 
considered later and is not mandatory.
The first hour of management, regardless of acute or chronic hyponatraemia, in the case of hypona-
traemia with severe symptoms is as follows:
150 mL 3% NaCl IV over 20 min followed by rechecking serum sodium and repeat infusion of another 
150 mL 3% NaCl. The 3% NaCl may be repeated until there is increase of 5 mmol/L in serum sodium 
concentration in the first hour; 1 mL of 3% NaCl contains 0.5 mmol of Na.
Our target is to increase serum sodium concentration by 10 mmol/L (alternative goal is 8 mmol/L) 
during the first 24 hr and try to increase by an additional 8 mmol/L during every 24 hr thereafter, 
until the serum sodium concentration reaches 130 mmol/L. Raising sodium by 4–6 mmol/L in the 
initial hours is enough to prevent brain herniation.
Serum sodium concentration should be checked every 6–12 hr in the first day and daily afterwards until 
the serum sodium concentration has stabilized.
If there is no improvement of symptoms after a 5 mmol/L increase in serum sodium concentration 
in the first hour, then continue infusion of 3% NaCl, aiming for an additional increase in serum 
sodium concentration, until the symptoms improve or serum sodium concentration increases 
10 mmol/L in total during 24 hr or the serum sodium concentration reaches 130 mmol/L.
Hyponatraemia with moderately severe symptoms:
◾
◾Prompt diagnostic assessment is started, and all the possible factors and medications (commonly 
diuretics) which can cause hyponatraemia are stopped and cause-specific treatment is started. 
Fluid restriction also is usually started.
◾
◾Immediate treatment is with a single IV infusion of 150 mL 3% NaCl over 20 min.
◾
◾Limit the increase in serum sodium concentration to 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hr and 8 mmol/L 
during every 24 hr thereafter until a serum sodium concentration of 130 mmol/L is achieved.
◾
◾Check serum sodium after 1, 6 and 12 hr.
◾
◾If serum sodium concentration further decreases despite treating the underlying cause, then it 
should be managed as in severely symptomatic hyponatraemia.
◾
◾In the case of euvolemic hyponatraemia, especially in heart failure and in certain subsets of SIADH, a 
vasopressin type 2 receptor antagonist (e.g., tolvaptan 15 mg one tablet is often enough) can be used in 
selected cases. Liver disease is a contraindication of tolvaptan therapy. It should not be given for 
more than 30 days. Urea, which is made palatable and suitable for oral ingestion, has also been 
proposed as a therapy.
◾
◾For those with new-onset symptoms with Na <130 mmol/L and known previous intracranial 
pathology like intracranial bleed, a 3% NaCl 100 mL bolus dose may be given. A repeat bolus may 
be given over 30 min if symptoms do not improve.
Acute Hyponatraemia without Severe or Moderately Severe Symptoms
First we must be sure that the value is correct.
Stop all the possible factors and medications which can cause hyponatraemia and start cause-spe-
cific treatment.

Swarup Paul and Sunandan Sikdar
4
If the acute decrease in serum sodium concentration exceeds 10 mmol/L, then a single IV infusion of 
150 mL 3% NaCl should be given over 20 minutes.
Check serum sodium concentration after 4 hr.
Treatment of Chronic Hyponatraemia
Chronic hyponatraemia (>120 mmol/L) with asymptomatic/mild symptoms: Fluid restriction (0.8–1 L/day), 
extra salt intake and avoidance of diuretics. One gram of salt is equivalent to 35 mL of 3% NaCl, 
and 9 g of salt are equal to 1 litre of 0.9% NaCl.
Chronic hyponatraemia (<120 mmol/L) with subtle symptoms: 3% NaCl @15 mL/hr for 10 hr. Then 
recheck sodium level.
Rapidly Reversible Cause of Hyponatraemia
There are three major causes:
a.	 True volume depletion: Volume correction may lead to water diuresis due to ADH suppression.
b.	 Hyponatraemia due to Addison disease: Injectable hydrocortisone may lead to rapid sodium rise 
due to suppression of ADH.
c.	 SIADH: Do not give isotonic saline. Fluid restriction is the treatment of choice. For severe cases 
3% NaCl is given. Loop diuretics and tolvaptan can be used in some cases.
Injectable desmopressin 1–2 mcg subcutaneously can be given 8-hourly for 24 hr, and with 3% NaCl 
may be given proactively in the cases noted earlier to prevent neurologic complications of rapid cor-
rection. Simultaneous fluid restriction is essential.
In most cases of symptomatic hyponatraemia except mild hypovolemic hyponatraemia, iso-
tonic saline is not useful, as the rate of correction is very slow (1 mmol/L for every litre of fluid 
infused).
  6.	What should be done if hyponatraemia is corrected too rapidly and why?
An important limitation of hyponatraemia correction formulae is that they are not sacrosanct, and 
frequently concomitant autocorrection occurs (e.g. administration of steroids in hypoadrenalism). 
Thus, the rate of correction may be faster than predicted.
Too rapid correction of hyponatraemia leads to osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS), espe-
cially if predisposing factors like alcoholism, malnutrition, liver disease and hypokalaemia 
are present. Chronic kidney disease (CKD), on the other hand, appears to be protective against 
ODS, and high urea may have a role. The pathology underlying ODS may be breakdown of the 
blood-brain barrier and microglia invasion. This mostly irreversible and often fatal disorder, 
typically manifests about 2–6 days after rapid correction of hyponatraemia. It is characterized by 
dysarthria, dysphagia, paraparesis or quadriparesis, behavioural disturbances, movement dis-
orders, seizures, lethargy, confusion, disorientation, obtundation and coma. Dysarthria occurs 
early with pontine involvement and persists. Dysphagia leads to aspiration. Corticospinal signs 
(hyperreflexia and bilateral Babinski signs) and corticobulbar signs (brisk jaw jerk) are common. 
Often MRI may be normal for the initial few weeks (often 4 weeks) and then shows central pon-
tine demyelination in half of the cases. In patients with hyponatraemia lasting more than 2 to 
3 days, or with hyponatraemia of unknown duration, the serum sodium must be raised by less 
than 6–8 mEq/L in any 24-hr period to prevent ODS. The risk of ODS is greatest in patients with 
a serum sodium of 120 mEq/L or less.
Prompt intervention for relowering the serum sodium concentration if it increases >10 mmol/L 
(8 mmol/L is also an alternative threshold) during the first 24 hr or >8 mmol/L in any 24 hr 
thereafter can be achieved by using 5% dextrose in water per 6 mL/kg lean body weight, infused 
over 2 hr.
Addition of IV desmopressin 2 mcg (it should not be given more than 8-hourly) for 24–48 hr may 
be considered if correction overshoots the safe limits (reactive strategy). This approach may also be 
started early (proactive strategy).
7.2  HYPERNATRAEMIA
  7.	 What is the definition of hypernatraemia?
Hypernatraemia is defined as serum Na+ concentration >145 mmol/L.

8.	What are the mechanism of hypernatraemia? (Table 7.1)

c.	 Excessive gain of hypertonic fluid
Chronic hypernatraemia (>48 hr) is more common and is usually caused in the intensive care unit

Diuretics to prevent volume overload
Free water administration
If hypovolemic or euvolemic, then check urine osmolality.

If urine osmolality >300 mOsm/kg, i.e., urine is concentrated (implies ADH is present), then it may

body weight will lower the serum sodium by approximately 1 mEq/L.
Or it may be due to osmotic diuresis (search underlying cause, replace free water to correct no faster 
than 0.5 mmol/L/hr).
If urine osmolality <300 mOsm/kg, i.e. dilute urine (or free water is being excreted), that means 
ADH is either absent or ineffective. Check for response to arginine vasopressin.
If it responds, then it is due to central diabetes insipidus; treat the patient with desmopressin acetate 
(ddAVP) at the dose of 10–40 mcg intranasally thrice daily in divided doses or 1–2 mcg SC/IV twice daily.
If it does not respond to ddAVP, then it is due to nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Treatment is to 
search for the underlying cause, a low-sodium diet with thiazide diuretics, a low-protein diet and 
nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

7.3  HYPOKALAEMIA
12.	What is hypokalaemia?
Hypokalaemia is defined as serum potassium <3.5 mEq/L.
13.	What are the causes of hypokalaemia?
1.	 Spurious (falsely increased): When there is extreme leucocytosis (WBC >1 lakh/cm3)
2.	 Decreased total body intake
a.	 Decreased intake
b.	 Increased K+ loss
i.	 Renal losses Renovascular or malignant hypertension 
Due to aldosterone-like effect: Cushing syndrome, Liddle syndrome, congenital adrenal 
hyperplasia
Aldosterone secondarily elevated: Bartter syndrome, Gitelman syndrome
ii.	 Extrarenal losses: Vomiting, diarrhoea, nasogastric suction
3.	 Transcellular shift: Alkalemia, insulin excess, beta-2 adrenergic agonist, stress, thyrotoxicosis, etc.
14.	How do you differentiate between renal and extrarenal losses?
Check urinary K+ or the transtubular K+ gradient (TTKG). If urinary K+ >20 mEq/l or TTKG>3, then 
it is considered a renal loss of serum K+. If urinary K+ <20 mEq/l or TTKG <3, then it is considered an 
extrarenal loss of serum K+.
15.	What is TTKG?
TTKG means transtubular K+ gradient and it is calculated as: (Urinary K/serum K)/(Urinary osmo-
lality/serum osmolality)
OR
(Urinary K+  × Serum osmolality)/(Serum K+ × Urine osmolality)
16.	What are the ECG changes of hypokalaemia?
1.	 ST-segment depression
2.	 Decrease in amplitude of T waves
3.	 Increase in amplitude of U wave (occurring at the end of T)
4.	 Premature atrial or ventricular ectopics
5.	 Sinus bradycardia
6.	 Atrioventricular block
7.	 Paroxysmal atrial or junctional tachycardia
8.	 Ventricular tachycardia (torsade de pointes)
9.	 Ventricular fibrillation
17.	 What is the treatment of hypokalaemia?
A proper history is essential: Correct reversible causes, which commonly are potassium-lowering 
drugs, urinary potassium loss and diarrhoea.
Discontinue diuretics and nebulization with salbutamol if they are responsible. Correct any mag-
nesium deficiency.
If the patient is symptomatic (arrhythmia, paralysis or weakness), then give intravenous K+ replace-
ment through a central venous line up to 40 mEq over 4 hr and continue ECG and serum K+ 
monitoring.
If the patient is asymptomatic, then check arterial blood gas (ABG); if it is metabolic acidosis, then 
give K+ citrate or K+ bicarbonate.
BK-TandF-SIKDAR_9781032455174-220973-Eresource_7.indd   7
17/02/23   9:32 AM
Swarup Paul and Sunandan Sikdar
8
If there is metabolic alkalosis or normal pH and the patient is normotensive, then give potassium 
chloride syrup orally.
If the patient is hypertensive with a normal pH or metabolic alkalosis, then potassium-sparing 
diuretics should be given.
7.4  HYPERKALAEMIA
18.	What is hyperkalaemia?
Hyperkalaemia is defined as a serum K+ level is >5 mEq/L.
19.	 What are the causes of hyperkalaemia?
1.	 Spurious: Platelet count >1,000,000/cm3, leucocytosis (WBC >50,000/cm3)
2.	 Impaired renal excretion of K+
i.	 Decreased glomerular filtration rate (GFR) (<20 mL/min): Retention of metabolic waste, K+  
supplementation, blood products, potassium-rich foods. Potassium also occurs in amoxycil-
lin clavulanate , is is often the cause of unexplained hyperkalemia in CCU
ii.	 Decreased aldosterone effect: Potassium-sparing diuretics, angiotensin-converting enzyme 
inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blocker, Type IV renal tubular acidosis, drugs (NSAIDs, 
ketoconazole, heparin, trimethoprim, cyclosporine, pentamidine)
3.	 Transcellular shift
i.	 Intracellular fluid–extracellular fluid (ICF-ECF) exchange: Beta adrenergic blockers, succinylcho-
line, insulin deficiency, digitalis intoxication
ii.	 Cellular release: Haemolysis, tumour lysis syndrome, rhabdomyolysis
20.	What are the ECG changes of hyperkalaemia?
1.	 Tall, peaked T waves with a shortened QT interval
2.	 Progressive lengthening of the PR interval and QRS duration
3.	 Disappearance of P waves
4.	 QRS widening and a sine wave pattern
5.	 Asystole and a flat ECG
See the chapter on ECG for correlation with blood levels of potassium.  The progression and sever-
ity of ECG changes do not correlate well with the serum potassium concentration; however, ECG 
changes are prominent once serum K >7 mmol/L.
21.	What is the treatment for hyperkalaemia?
Prompt initiation of emergency treatment should be considered once K >6.5 mmol/L and symptoms 
related to hyperkalaemia (weakness, rhythm abnormalities) and changes in the ECG occur. Patients 
with underlying acidosis will deteriorate rapidly. Often the ABG may be an initial guide. The most 
common underlying cause is kidney disease and drugs (combined use of telmisartan or ramipril 
with spironolactone).
A.	 To stabilize membrane potential
i.	 Inject calcium gluconate 10 mL 10% (1000 mg) over 10 min IV through a central vein. The 
effect of intravenous calcium administration begins within minutes but is relatively short-
lived (30–60 min). Hence, supplemental therapies are needed. If no improvement of ECG by 
5 min, then repeat the dose.
B.	 Drive potassium inside cells
i.	 Insulin: Insulin activates the Na-K-ATPase pump in skeletal muscle, thus driving potassium 
inside cells. Ten units of regular insulin in 100 mL of 25% dextrose is given to normoglycae-
mic patients or can be given in well-controlled hyperglycaemic patients. If capillary blood 
glucose (CBG)>250 mg/dL, then give insulin alone. The potassium-lowering effect is in the 
range of 1 mEq/L. It takes about 15 minutes to show its potassium-lowering effect, and its 
action lasts for 6–8 hr.
BK-TandF-SIKDAR_9781032455174-220973-Eresource_7.indd   8
17/02/23   9:32 AM

9
ii.	 Salbutamol or albuterol: Beta-2 agonists work by the same Na+-K+-ATPase pump pathway 
described earlier. Ten to twenty milligrams dissolved in 4 mL of saline (4–8 times the bron-
chodilation dose), given by nebulized inhalation over 15 min, can decrease the serum potas-
sium level 1–1.5 mEq/L. The onset of action is about 10–30 min, and this effect lasts for 
3–6 hr.
iii.	 Sodium bicarbonate: Use of bicarbonate in bolus form is applicable only if severe acidosis (pH 
<7.1) is concomitantly present. Bicarbonate infusion may be a more effective form than bolus. 
Volume load in the case of underlying heart failure is a concern. Three ampoules (total 150 
mEq) of sodium bicarbonate should be dissolved in 1 litre of 5% dextrose and given as an 
infusion over 2–4 hr (or run at the rate of 2–4 mEq/min in drip) until bicarbonate normal-
izes. Its onset of action is 4 hr, and it may last for more than 6 hr. It reduces potassium about 
0.5–0.75 mEq/L.
C.	 Drive potassium out of the body
i.	 Loop diuretics: The dose is variable and depends upon the GFR. Injectable furosemide 40 mg 
IV followed by infusion is commonly used. The potassium-lowering effect is variable, and 
onset of action is 30–60 min; the action lasts for 4–6 hr but should not be given in volume-
depleted patients.
ii.	 Sodium polystyrene sulphonate (SPS): This cation exchanger is used as follows: 25–50 mg are 
mixed in 100 mL 20% sorbitol administered orally or 50 g are mixed in 200 mL 30% sorbi-
tol and given rectally. Onset of action is within 1–2 hr, and its action lasts for 4–6 hr. The 
potassium-lowering magnitude is about 0.5–1 mEq/L. 
SPS with or without sorbitol should not be given to the following patients because they 
may be at high risk for intestinal necrosis:
–	
Postoperative patients
–	
Patients with an ileus or who are receiving opiates
–	
Patients with a large or small bowel obstruction
–	
Patients with underlying bowel disease, e.g., ulcerative colitis or Clostridioides (formerly 
Clostridium) difficile colitis
Better alternatives like patiromer (8.4 g, repeated daily as needed) or zirconium cyclo-
silicate (10 g three times daily for 48 hr) can be used instead of SPS.
iii.	 Haemodialysis: Onset of action is immediate and lasts until dialysis completion. Requirement 
of dialysis is variable. Reduction of potassium depends upon dialysis dose and dialysate.

8  Haemodynamics
Sunandan Sikdar and Swarup Paul
  1.	How do automated blood pressure cuffs work?
Automated blood pressure cuffs work on the basis of oscillometry. While traditional blood pres­
sure cuffs determine the systolic and diastolic pressure from Korotkoff sounds, the automated cuff 
works on the principle that the amplitude of sensed oscillation is a maximum at mean blood pres­
sure. Thus, they measure mean blood pressure. The systolic and diastolic blood pressures are not mea­
sured directly; they are derived from the rate of change in the oscillation amplitude based upon 
proprietary algorithms. Thus, measurement errors may occur in arrhythmia, very low or very high 
blood pressure, motion artefacts and a cuff of inappropriate size.
  2.	What factors affect the waveform recorded by the pressure monitoring system?
Like all waves, the pressure waveform (Figure 8.1) is a periodic fluctuation of force per unit area 
and can be resolved into waves of fundamental frequency (ff, cycles per second, at HR of 60/min, it 
is 60/60 or 1 Hz) along with its multiples (called harmonics, may be like 2, 3, 5 … Hz, etc.). The physi­
ologic information is contained in the ff and its first 10 harmonics. Thus, at an HR of 120/min, the 
ff is 120/60, or 2 Hz and the 10th harmonic is 20 Hz.
Three factors determine the crispness of the waveform: Natural frequency of the system, 
amplitude ratio and damping. These are of crucial importance in invasive arterial monitoring.
The natural frequency (nf) is the frequency at which a system (e.g. the components of a pressure 
transducer) naturally vibrates once it has been set into motion in the absence of friction. For a system 
to reproduce a distortion-free arterial pressure waveform with faithful reproduction of detail, when 
the heart rate is 120 beats/min, the transducer should have a frequency greater than the 10th harmonic 
of the waveform, i.e., 20 Hz. The larger the bore (increased radius) of the tubing and the shorter its 
length, less the compliance (no bubbles), less the density of the fluid (no blood) — higher the natural 
frequency of the system. When the nf of the system approaches the ff of the waveform, the output sig­
nal augments dramatically compared to the input signal. In order to maintain a proportional ampli­
tude, a system of dissipation of energy is required, called damping. Optimal damping dissipates the 
energy of the vibration gradually and maintains a flat frequency response curve.
The amplitude ratio is the ratio of output vs input signal. It should be constant over a broad range 
of frequencies (also called frequency response – imagine if the ratio changes with HR, the waveform 
depicted in the monitor would get distorted). A stiff transducer membrane has a good frequency 
response. A flaccid membrane cannot pick up higher harmonics and distorts the waveform.
The dampening coefficient (must be ~0.5–0.6) quantifies the frictional forces that absorb energy 
and determine how quickly a signal decays back to baseline. An underdamped system overreacts 
to the pressure curve and gives rise to sharp/exaggerated systolic peaks and diastolic troughs. 
This leads to systolic and pulse pressure overestimation and diastolic pressure underestimation. 
Underdampening can be reduced by using longer and thinner tubing. An overdamped system, on the 
other hand, leads to loss of detail in the waveform and erroneously low systolic and pulse pressure.

Overdampening occurs with additional tubing, stopcocks, air bubbles or blood clots in the system. 
To reduce the likelihood of overdamping, use of a short, stiff, non-compliant tubing and limiting the 
number of three-way valves are suggested.
However, in both overdamping and underdamping, the mean BP approximates to the actual 
mean BP.
  3.	What is a bedside flush test?
The valve of the continuous flush system must be pulled to generate a square wave on the output trac­
ing. By releasing the valve, a variable number of undershot and overshot waves can be observed that 
will decay exponentially in accordance with the damping coefficient. Two measures are necessary:
	
Natural frequency = Paper speed (mm/sec)/Distance between successive peaks (mm)
of the return waves, e.g., 25 (mm/sec)/1.7 mm = 14.7 Hz
The damping coefficient can be derived by calculating the amplitude ratio (dividing the amplitude 
of the second oscillation by the first, damped/normal amplitude), e.g., 16 mm/22 mm = 0.72.
  4.	Where is the zero reference?
The axis is the reference or zero line corresponding to the middle point between the sternum and 
the back (5 cm below the sternum), at the left fourth intercostal space. The transducer should be 
positioned at the level of this space at the bedside. This is actually the level of the left ventricle and 
aorta in the supine position.
  5.	What haemodynamic information is obtained by changes in the arterial pressure waveform?
The pulse contour is the result of wave reflections from arterial bifurcations and high-resistance 
peripheral arterioles. The main point of reflection is the distal aorta. The more one goes to the 
periphery from the central aorta, the earlier the peak pressure is reached.
The normal waveform (Figure 8.2A,B) consists of a temporal sequence of systolic upstroke, sys­
tolic peak, systolic decline, a small hump of the reflected wave, dicrotic notch, diastolic runoff and 
end-diastolic pressure.

vasoconstriction.
Reduced systolic and diastolic pressures and a delayed and low dicrotic notch suggest severe 
vasodilatation (e.g., sepsis, vasovagal reflex, nitrate administration), as a longer time is needed for 
the aortic pressure to exceed the ventricular pressure. However, if low pressure is associated with 
an early dicrotic notch, the possibility of volume loss with peripheral vasoconstriction should be 
kept in mind.
In cases of shock, except during acute inflammation, diastolic waves are often increased when 
hypotension is compensated for by peripheral vasoconstriction.
In aortic stenosis, the wave contour is rounded (pulsus parvus) due to the slow ejection 
and the dicrotic notch is less prominent. In aortic regurgitation, the reverse occurs – the wave­
form is characterized by a steep rise of the systolic upstroke, low diastolic and wide pulse 
pressure.
Alternation of beats with higher and lower pulse pressures is indicative of severe left ventricular 
dysfunction, called pulsus alternans. The augmented beat is due to the extra preload caused by 
excess blood remaining from the previous ejection.
In pulsus paradoxus, the rise of systolic blood pressure (SBP) in expiration and the fall in inspira­
tion is exaggerated and is a characteristic feature of cardiac tamponade.
During positive pressure mechanical ventilation, the following changes occur: During 
inspiration due to increased pulmonary inflow into the left atrium (LA), left ventricle (LV) 
and reduced afterload, the stroke volume of LV, and hence the SBP, increases. During 
expiration due to pulmonary sequestration of blood, the SBP falls. If the difference of maxi­
mum SBP and the minimum SBP (called the systolic pressure variation) is more than 15%, 
provided there is no spontaneous breath or arrhythmia, a fluid challenge to treat hypotension 
is reasonable.
  6.	What are the uses of central venous pressure (CVP)?
Use of CVP has declined, but where it is being used it provides:
a.	 An idea of volume status; though this measurement has its pitfalls, response to fluid challenge 
and measurement during progressive hypotension does give some clues. CVP represents right 
atrium (RA) pressure and, by extension, right ventricle (RV) diastolic pressure in the absence of 
tricuspid stenosis.
b.	 The CVP waveforms have diagnostic value.
c.	 The line can be used to deliver fluids and drugs. It can be used to sample mixed venous O2 
saturation in those without a pulmonary catheter (ScVO2). ScVO2 >70% in septic shock is a use­
ful target.
  7.	 Where is the zero of CVP?
At the mid-point of the RA. A good approximation of this point is a vertical distance 5 cm below 
the sternal angle, where the second rib meets the sternum. This level is valid whether the subject 
is supine or sitting up. In practice, however, the transducer is levelled to the mid-thoracic position. 
This results in values ~3 mmHg higher than those based on the sternal angle, with the precise dif­
ference varying with chest size.
  8.	What are the waves of CVP?
The CVP tracing has three distinguishable upward waves:
a – atrial contraction
•	 Significance: Canon a wave – complete heart block
Tall a – Tricuspid stenosis
c – Bellowing up of tricuspid valve at onset of ventricular systole
v – RA filling
•	 Significance: Tall v wave – severe tricuspid regurgitation

The two downward waves are:
“x” – descent due to atrial relaxation
“y” – due to atrial emptying during the early phase of diastole

–

–

9.	Where do you measure CVP?
In normal CVP, the a and v are large waves with a > v. The c wave is a minute deflection on the 
descending limb of the ‘a’ wave coinciding with the end of QRS on the ECG on the monitor. The 
CVP should be measured at the c wave in end expiration. An alternative is the base of the ‘a’ 
wave.
10.	How do you interpret CVP?
In normal sitting subjects, CVP is sub-atmospheric, yet there is no need to give fluid. The value 
of CVP by itself is most useful in the negative sense. A high CVP indicates that fluid boluses are 
unlikely to be helpful. CVP measurements can assist in assessing the response to a fluid challenge. 
For practical purposes, the increase in CVP should be ≥2 mmHg on fluid bolus, as this can be read­
ily identified on a monitor. If there is no inspiratory fall in CVP, it is unlikely that the patient will 
be fluid-responsive. Respiratory swings of CVP give an idea about inspiratory efforts and lung 
compliance.
11.	What is a high CVP?
The plateau of the cardiac function curve usually occurs at values <10 mmHg (13–14 mmHg if using 
the mid-thoracic level). Without any measure of cardiac output, it is thus reasonable to target a CVP 
of 10 mmHg, as recommended in early goal-directed resuscitation protocols.
12.	How does pulse oximetry work?
Oximetry is the measurement of oxyhaemoglobin in blood as a percentage of haemoglobin 
(Hb) species. The absorption of light is proportional to chromatophore concentration (Beer’s 
law) and the thickness of the transmitting layer (Lambert’s law). The differing absorption of 
light (emitted by two light-emitting diodes [LEDs] with wavelengths 660 nm red and 940 nm 
infrared) by two different species of Hb (oxy Hb and deoxy Hb) is measured by a photodiode. 
The transmitted and reflected signal is digitalized and the difference between systolic and 
diastolic measured to give a pulsatile component (ac) and non-pulsatile component (dc), there­
fore allowing for quantification of absorption due to tissue, venous blood and nail polish (this 
is the dc component). Finally, the ratio (R) is obtained as follows: (ac 660/ac 940)/(dc 940/dc 660). 
This R is then compared by the software to a standard table (SpO2 of human volunteers breath­
ing various known concentration of oxygen) to determine the SpO2. Thus, SpO2 is 94%, which 
means that 94% of the patients’ haemoglobin is oxy Hb at that FiO2 and oxygen flow. The probe 
calculates SpO2 about 25 times/sec, rejects artefacts and determines the average of SpO2 over 
3–12 sec and updates the screen every 1–2 sec. Information about heart rate and pulse contour 
is also obtained.
13.	What is the lag time for a drop in SpO2 when FiO2 is reduced?
The lag time is 10 sec for ear probes and 50 sec for finger probes.
14.	What are the limitation of pulse oximeters?
a.	 Methaemoglobin (Met Hb) and carboxy Hb (COHb) cannot be determined, even though they 
may be producing hypoxia. Pulse oximeters read HbCO as mostly HbO2 and over-read SO2 by 
1% for every 1% of COHb in the blood. For reading this, co-oximeters (using multiple wave­
lengths of light) are required.
b.	 Hypoperfusion reduces the accuracy of the SpO2 measurement, and this is a common problem 
in the cardiac care unit (CCU) where patients are frequently on pressors.
8  Haemodynamics
67
c.	 They are insensitive to large changes in PaO2 in the high PaO2 range.
d.	 When the skin is cold or in presence of strong light, SpO2 may be low.
e.	 Methylene blue and indocyanine green absorb red light, artificially lowering SpO2.
f.	 MRI and cautery may interfere with SpO2.
15.	What are the markers of tissue hypoxia?
The ultimate common pathway of different aetiologies of shock is tissue hypoxia. It is defined 
as inadequate oxygen delivery compared to demand of metabolically active tissue. Normally 
in the presence of adequate oxygen, cellular glycolysis generates pyruvate, which enters mito­
chondria and participates in the Krebs cycle generating NADPH and FADH; these in turn 
generate adenosine triphosphate (ATP) by the electron transport chain using oxygen (36 ATP/
cycle). When oxygen is inadequate, electron transport suffers, leading to mitochondrial dys­
function, and excess pyruvate is accumulated in the cell by anaerobic glycolysis (2 ATP/cycle). 
This pyruvate is converted to l-lactate by lactate dehydrogenase (d-lactate is found in intestinal 
flora). This lactate diffuses out of the cell and increases blood lactate levels (when haemody­
namics are normal, part of it is taken up by the liver, and through the Cori cycle it is converted 
back to glucose – this beneficial mechanism is reduced in shock). Further in shock-like situa­
tions, oxygen extraction by capillaries becomes maximum, leading to decreased venous oxy­
gen and widening of the arteriovenous oxygen difference.
Thus, the markers of tissue hypoxia are actually the markers of global hypoperfusion, as non-inva­
sive measurement of tissue hypoxia is difficult in clinical practice:
a.	 ScVO2 (venous saturation from central line) <70%
b.	 l-Lactate >3 mEq/L
c.	 P (v-a) CO2 (veno-arterial CO2 difference) >6 mmHg

glycolysis. Analysis should be done within 15 min; otherwise, storage must be at <4°C or the use of 
fluoride oxalate tubes should be ensured.

9  The Role and Interpretation of Biomarkers
Sunandan Sikdar, Barnik Chaudhuri, and Arijita Mukherjee
  1.	What is a biomarker?
A biomarker is noninvasive (usually body fluid-based) tool that reproducibly indicates the diagno-
sis or severity of one or more pathophysiological processes.
  2.	What are cardiac biomarkers?
Cardiac biomarkers are listed in Table 9.1.
  3.	What are the precautions during blood sampling for biomarkers?
Troponin values will depend on, if the sample is heparinized or not. A heparinized sample was 
used in the LITROP study for both hs-Trop T and Trop I. Brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) is usually 
collected in ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) vials, and they should be preserved with ice. 
BNP degrades quite rapidly and can give false-negative results. On the other hand, NT-Pro BNP is 
relatively stable.
  4.	What is troponin?
A contractile unit of sarcomere contains thick filaments (myosin) and thin filaments (actin). The 
troponin-tropomyosin complex localized on actin regulates the calcium-induced interaction of actin 
and myosin, which is the basis of heart muscle shortening. Troponin C binds calcium, troponin T 
is the link between tropomyosin and actin and troponin I inhibits cross-bridge formation when 
calcium is absent.
  5.	What are the non-cardiac causes of disproportionately raised troponin?
That pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension and aortic dissection will cause raised 
levels is expected, but the more surprising among the list includes both hypothyroidism and 
CLINICAL PEARL: CAN TROPONIN BE RAISED IN NORMAL 
INDIVIDUALS WITHOUT ISCHAEMIC HEART DISEASE?
As assays have become more and more sensitive, cardiac troponin can be detected even in 
normal population. In fact, sensitive assays can detect troponin in 20%–50% of the normal 
population, while highly sensitive assays can detect troponin in 50%–90% of healthy indi-
viduals. At what troponin level it will be labelled as pathological elevation is given as the 
99th percentile of that particular assay by the respective manufacturer. This means that if the 
blood level exceeds that particular concentration only in one out of 100 individuals it will be 
false positive – that is a healthy person is misdiagnosed. Even with this cut-off it, is estimated 
that 20% of emergency room troponin-positive cases will fail to be finally labelled as acute 
coronary syndrome.

hyperthyroidism; any critical illness, including sepsis and burns; infiltrative diseases, including

haemorrhage. So, in chest pain with ECG changes and raised troponin, each member of the big three – 
acute coronary syndrome (ACS), aortic dissection and pulmonary embolism – should be considered. 
Troponin is an organ-specific marker of myocardial injury, not a disease-specific marker. So, ECG, 
echocardiogram and symptoms should to be considered prior to a diagnosis of ACS.
  6.	What type of assay is used in measuring troponin?
Non-competitive enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs) based on the sandwich principle, 
using a capture antibody and a detection antibody (which attaches to a signal system). These anti­
bodies bind the troponin fragments of the serum.
  7.	 What is the advantage of hs-troponin over previous assays?
Introduction of hs-troponin has reduced the troponin-blind window while diagnosing myocardial 
infarction (MI). The rise is quite rapid, and serial measurement at 1 or 3 hours may suffice rather than 
waiting for 6 hours (Figure 9.1). Instead of considering troponin as a binary (positive or negative) bio­
marker, considering the absolute level and rate of rise is more appropriate. The larger the absolute level 
or the rate of rise, the more certain the diagnosis of ischaemia. However, if there is severe angina with 
ST elevation on the ECG, one must not wait for troponin, high sensitivity or otherwise.
  8.	What are the disadvantages of the newer-generation assays?
By convention, the 99th percentile has been used as the cut-off based on a reference normal popula­
tion. However, confusion arises as cTnI has different 99th percentile values from different manufac­
turers. Further, while evaluating acute chest pain, one in five patients will have discordant results 
between troponin T and troponin I.
  9.	 What are the requirements for labelling a troponin assay as high sensitivity?
The coefficient of variation (CV) of troponin assays should be <10% at the 99th percentile upper 
reference limit in a normal population, and they need to measure concentrations above their limit of 
detection in >50% of a normal reference population. Sex-neutral cut-off of hs-troponin T is 14 ng/L 
and of hs-troponin I is 26 ng/mL (men have a higher cut-off than women). There is no circadian 
variation of levels of this marker.
10.	What is the prognostic import of troponin?
Rise of troponin confers an adverse prognosis. In heart failure (HF), coronary artery disease, chronic 
kidney disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension, raised troponin signifies worse outcomes.

Rise of troponin in kidney disease may be due to both increased release and decreased clearance. 
Preoperative or postoperative rise of troponin in relation to non-cardiac surgery portends increased 
30-day mortality. Nearly 90% of these patients have no chest pain, and this is usually a silent event. 
Thus, it may be prudent to get a preoperative and postoperative day 1 and day 2 troponin level in 
patients who are elderly (>65 years) or those with vascular risk factors.
11.	What is the mechanism of release of troponin from cytosol?
There is a biphasic release of troponin (Figures 9.1 and 9.2) during ischaemia – the initial peak is 
due to release from the injured sarcomere’s cytosolic pool (predominately free troponin T) and the 
later sustained phase from degradation of contractile apparatus (by the enzymes calpain, caspase 
and metalloproteinase). The latter phase indicates the extent of infarct. Thus after ischaemic insult, 
different forms of troponin are detected – free-form (4%–6%), binary and ternary forms.
12.	What are the biomarkers for HF?
The natriuretic peptides are the established biomarkers for HF: BNP and NT-pro-BNP. The pep­
tide is predominantly released from ventricular myocardium in response to stretch as a prohor­
mone, pro-BNP. Half of this undergoes cleavage to active fragment BNP by neural endopeptidases 
and the other half cleaves to NT-pro-BNP. The BNP binds to the NPR-A receptor to counteract the 
renin-angiotensin and sympathetic system effects by cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP). The 
NT-pro-BNP undergoes renal clearance. The BNP has a shorter half-life (20 min) compared with 
NT-pro-BNP (120 min).
13.	What are the biological factors affecting natriuretic peptide levels?
Higher BNP levels are found in the elderly. Pathological states like renal failure and pulmonary 
hypertension/pulmonary embolism can cause raised BNP levels. In patients treated by the drug 
sacubitril-valsartan BNP levels may be falsely high, and NT-pro-BNP should be used to tailor ther­
apy. In flash pulmonary oedema (1- to 2-hr symptom onset) and rarely in acute mitral regurgitation, 
the BNP level may be falsely low.
14.	What are the normal cut-offs for natriuretic peptide measurements?
For the test, a 5-cc sample is taken in an EDTA (1 mg/mL) vial and measured by fluorescence immu­
noassay. BNP: <35 pg/mL (non-acute), <100 pg/mL (acute), NT-pro-BNP: <125 pg/mL (<75 years, 
non-acute), <450 pg/mL (>75 years, non-acute), <300 pg/mL (acute). In the BASEL study (2004) in 
acute dyspnoea in the emergency department (ED), the rule-out value of BNP for HF was <100 
pg/mL and the rule-in value >500 pg/mL. In the PRIDE study (2005) the HF rule in cut-offs for 
NT-pro-BNP were >450 pg/mL for <50 years and >900 pg/mL for >50 years. The rule-out HF value 
for NT-pro-BNP is conventionally <300 pg/mL. For BNP values between 100 and 500 pg/mL right

15.	What are the non-cardiac causes of disproportionately raised BNP?
The more important causes are age, liver disease, sepsis, subarachnoid haemorrhage, stroke, trauma 
and anaemia.
16.	What are the causes of disproportionately low BNP?
They include obesity and flash pulmonary oedema (1–2 hours). Pericardial diseases are character­
ized by dyspnoea with low BNP levels.
17.	 What are the diagnostic and prognostic import of BNP?
If the level of BNP/NT-pro-BNP is above the cut-off and symptoms/signs of HF are present, then 
echocardiography-guided left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) <40%, 40%–49% and >50% 
defines the entities of HF with reduced EF (HFrEF), HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) and HF 
with preserved EF (HFpEF), respectively. Raised BNP reliably predicts restrictive cardiomyopathy 
and rules out constrictive pericarditis. The level of BNP after treatment has been taken as a marker 
of clinical improvement across various studies.
18.	What is the role of D-dimer?
Fibrinogen is converted by thrombin (Figure 9.3) to fibrin monomers, which undergo cross-linking 
to form polymers, a state that is stabilized by factor XIII. Plasmin degrades the fibrin network to gen­
erate D-dimers (two D subunits linked together). D-dimer is named from the D subunit of fibrino­
gen (fibrinogen has one D subunit flanking an E subunit, D-E-D).
19.	 What are the methods and cut-off values of D-dimer measurement?
D-dimer is measured by any of (1) whole-blood agglutination assays (semiquantitative positive/
negative) – this has low sensitivity and should be avoided; (2) enzyme-linked immunosorbent 
(Figure 9.3) or immunofluorescent assays (ELISA and ELFA, respectively); and (3) latex aggluti­
nation assays (immunoturbidometric method). Often the numerical results of different meth­
ods/manufacturers are not comparable. D-dimer has high sensitivity but poor specificity for the 
detection of venous thromboembolism.

The normal cut-off is <500 mcg/L for <50 years; for age >50 years, the cut-off is 10 times the

20.	What is the diagnostic importance of D-dimer?
It is predominately used in diagnosing venous thromboembolism (VTE), particularly in those with 
a low probability of VTE. It lacks specificity and can be raised in pregnancy, puerperium, chronic 
inflammatory conditions and hospital inpatients. Hence, in these conditions testing for D-dimer is 
rarely of value and imaging tests should be used.
However, it may also be of help in ruling out aortic dissection in low-risk patients (cut-off <500 
mcg/L) and in disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).
In women with maintenance anticoagulation after an index VTE, a negative D-dimer can be used 
to decide when to stop anticoagulation after a proper time.
21.	What are the biomarkers of aortic dissection?
Markers related to vascular smooth muscle (smooth muscle myosin), the interstitium (calponin), 
the elastic lamina (elastin), endothelial cells and blood-nonintima interactions (D-dimer) have been 
studied. D-dimer and an interleukin receptor family member, soluble ST2 (sST2), has been found to 
have clinical utility. A cut-off value of sST2 <34.6 ng/mL has been suggested to rule out aortic dis­
section in acute chest pain patients.

10  Acute Chest Pain
Sunandan Sikdar and Mrinal Kanti Das
10.1  INTRODUCTION
Acute chest pain is a very important symptom in the cardiovascular system. A thorough clinical 
history and examinations at the emergency room (ER) can offer a lot of inputs regarding the aetiol­
ogy. However, there is always the need for supporting investigations to clinch the cause. The fol­
lowing discussion in the format of questions is an attempt to arrive at the appropriate diagnosis of 
acute chest pain.
  1.	What are the characteristics of ischaemic chest pain?
Differentiating angina or ischaemic pain from non-ischaemic ones is of paramount importance in 
the cardiac care unit (CCU). However, in the elderly and in women, it is often difficult to differenti­
ate. In diabetics the chest pain may be absent. The special characteristics of chest pain may be clari­
fied using OLD CAAR mnemonic.
a.	 Onset: Sudden (acute coronary syndrome [ACS])/gradual (underlying chronic stable angina)
b.	 Location: Retrosternal
c.	 Duration: >20 min in the case of ACS, <10 min suggests relatively stable
d.	 Character: Deep and dull
e.	 Aggravating factors: At rest suggests ACS; on exertion suggest stable angina syndrome
f.	 Associated symptoms: Dyspnoea/sweating/syncope
g.	 Radiation: Arm
Chest pain should not be labelled as typical or atypical; rather, it should be labelled as cardiac, pos­
sibly cardiac or non-cardiac. In patients of 75 years of age or more, ACS should be suspected if there 
is dyspnoea, syncope or delirium along with pain (AHA 2021).
  2.	What is the differential diagnosis of acute chest pain and the identifying features?
The identifying features are shown in Table 10.1.
