  8.	How do you treat CRS 1?
Treatment of CRS Type 1 is mainly symptomatic, and there is no disease-modifying therapy at pres-
ent that can change the disease course or the end outcome. However, in patients with acute heart 
failure and renal dysfunction, there is an important difference in diuretic sensitivity (they usually 
have decreased sensitivity to diuretics) and drug dosing than patients with normal renal function, 
which should be kept in mind while handling such cases.
Although there is no definitive therapy for CRS 1, thankfully improvement of cardiac status her-
alds the recovery of renal function in most cases.
At the outset the volume-overloaded patients (the majority) must be separated from volume-
depleted ones. Judicious diuresis of volume-overloaded patients to achieve euvolemic status can 
cause a further rise in urea and apparent worsening of renal function, but studies (ESCAPE, 
EVEREST) have shown that clinical outcomes and survival improve after discharge. Patients with 
acute heart failure and renal dysfunction often show further worsening of renal function while on 
decongestive therapy; however, if there is progressive clinical improvement, usually this renal func-
tion worsening is not associated with any ultimately adverse outcome.
The DOSE trial did not establish superiority of continuous diuretic infusion over intermittent 
bolus doses or high dose (>2.5 times total the daily outpatient dose) over low dose (= total daily 
outpatient dose). We usually use a continuous infusion of furosemide @ 1–5 mg/hr (depending on 
the clinical situation). Higher doses are required if creatinine is >3 mg/dL, and lower doses are used 
if there is a risk of hypotension.
Patients with left ventricular (LV) dysfunction are intuitively thought to be hypotension 
prone. But it is possible that, because the heart works in the flat part of the Frank-Starling 
(volume-pressure) curve in LV systolic dysfunction, decreasing preload by diuresis does not 
significantly reduce cardiac output and hence blood pressure. The blood pressure reduction 
may rather indicate that overdiuresis has taken place and the patient is volume depleted at that 
point. The reduction of cardiac output by diuresis is more likely to occur in preserved ejec-
tion fraction where the curve is steeper (a small decrease in volume causes a large decrease in 
pressure).
The initial enthusiasm about ultrafiltration as a key method of fluid removal in ADHF, which was 
kindled by the UNLOAD trial, was dampened by the CARESS trial. In this trial, medical diuresis 
was as effective as ultrafiltration but with fewer adverse effects. Currently, ultrafiltration is the ther-
apy of choice for those with ADHF with advanced renal disease or oliguria or ADHF unresponsive 
to intravenous diuretics.
Vasodilators (which counter neurohormonal vasoconstriction in ADHF) like nitroglycerin or 
nitroprusside do not add any benefit over and above blood pressure lowering when added to diuret-
ics. The hope about using natriuretic peptides like nesiritide for vasodilation and diuresis (unlike 
angiotensin receptor/neprilysin inhibitors [ARNIs] in chronic heart failure) in ADHF was not borne 
out by the ASCEND-HF and ROSE trials. This drug was not superior to intravenous diuretics but 
caused more hypotension.
Thus, treatment of CRS 1 is primarily supportive.
  9.	 What are the preventive measures for CRS 1?
The following measures provide an idea on the precautionary steps:
1.	 Minimize contrast volume
2.	 Maintain euvolaemia
3.	 Avoid nephrotoxic drugs
4.	 Avoid hypotension
5.	 Minimize use of vasopressors as far as possible
10.	How does iodinated contrast cause renal injury?
These agents induce intense and prolonged vasoconstriction at the corticomedullary junction of 
the kidney (often mediated by adenosine and endothelin) and directly impair the autoregulatory 
capacity of the kidney through a reduction in nitric oxide synthesis. This may lead to ischaemic 
renal injury and acute kidney injury (AKI). There is also direct tubular injury by iodinated contrast, 
which may cause in rare cases acute tubular necrosis and AKI.

Sunandan Sikdar and Pinaki Mukhopadhyay

11.	What is contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN)?
After contrast administration, an increase in serum creatinine (SCr) over baseline by 48 hr, such as 
>25% above baseline or an absolute increase of >0.0.5 mg/dL, has been labelled as CIN in the litera-
ture. CIN is the third leading cause of all cases of hospital-acquired renal failure. The risk of CIN 
varies from 2%–30% in unselected patients undergoing cardiovascular angiographic procedures. It 
is associated with a significant increase in patient morbidity and mortality. Nowadays commonly 
used the low osmolar non-ionic agent iohexol (Omnipaque) and iso-osmolar non-ionic agent iodixa-
nol (Visipaque) cause less CIN than the previously used ionic agent ioxaglate.
12.	What are the risk factors of CIN?
Age >75 years, diabetes, previous kidney disease, HF, shock, sepsis, volume depletion and con-
comitant use of nephrotoxic medications are important risk factors. However, the volume of contrast 
used may be one of the most important factors.
13.	What is the threshold contrast volume?
Usually a total dose of <30 mL for diagnostic studies and <100 mL for interventional procedures 
lessens the risk for CIN. The upper limit of contrast volume is given by the empirical formula 
(Cigarroa et al c. 1989) of 5 cc × body weight (numerical value in kg)/SCr in mg/dL.
14.	How do you prevent CIN?
Before sending for an interventional procedure, the steps that should be followed by the intensive 
care physician are:
1.	 Identify risk: Low-risk eGFR >60 mL/min/1.73 m2, high risk <eGFR 60 mL/min/1.73 m2
There is a high-risk for eGFR <60 in the case of intraarterial contrast and eGFR <45 in the case 
of IV contrast.
2.	 Withhold nephrotoxic medications.
3.	 Hydration (judicious in low LV ejection fraction [LVEF]), especially if eGFR <60 mL/min:
•	 Recommended fluid therapy for admitted patients: IV isotonic saline 1 mL/kg/hr for 6–12 hr prior 
to the procedure and 6–12 hr after the procedure.
•	 For OPD patients, fluid therapy can be adjusted to a target of 3 mL/kg of fluid over 1 hr prior 
to the procedure and 6 mL/kg fluid over 2–6 hr after the procedure.
4.	 Administer N-acetylcysteine (NAC): 1200 mg administered orally q12hr × four doses beginning 
prior to contrast. Previously it was believed that NAC acts by free radical scavenging, prevent-
ing glutathione depletion and causing vasodilatation. However, large trials failed to show any 
benefit, and at present it is not recommended in either the prevention or treatment of CIN.
5.	 Ascorbic acid has also limited data for this indication, 3 g orally prior to the procedure and 2 g 
orally twice daily for the day after. There is no beneficial role; hence, it is not recommended.
6.	 Sodium bicarbonate (limited data): Use optional
i.	 154 mEq/l @ 3 mL/kg/hr starting 1 hr before contrast
ii.	 154 mEq/L @ 1 mL/kg/hr for 6 hr following contrast
There is no beneficial role; hence, it is not recommended.
7.	 Measure SCr 48 hr after contrast exposure.
8.	 Minimize contrast volume as far as possible: Use a small catheter size, biplane or rotational coronary 
angiography and avoid left ventriculography. The only interventions that have been proven 
effective in preventing CIN are:
a.	 IV hydration with isotonic saline prior to and after the procedure
b.	 Use of a low osmolar contrast agent
15.	What is the role of dialysis in CIN?
For advanced CKD, pre- and post-procedure haemodialysis is usually done, but there is no clini-
cal evidence that prophylactic dialysis reduces the risk of AKI, even when carried out within 1 hr 
BK-TandF-SIKDAR_9781032455174-220973-Eresource_43.indd   4
29/03/23   3:09 PM
43  Cardiorenal Syndrome and Heart-Kidney Interactions
5
or simultaneously with contrast administration. While dialysis is lifesaving, it also is a marker 
for a poor prognosis. Studies have shown that percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) patients 
with CIN not requiring dialysis have an in-hospital mortality of 7%, which increases to 35% if they 
require dialysis.
There is no role for prophylactic dialysis or hemofiltration in preventing CIN.
16.	What are the novel biomarkers of AKI?
Since SCr is an insensitive and a late marker of CRS and AKI, there is a requirement for more sensi-
tive biomarkers to fill the gap. Neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin and cystatin C are emerg-
ing biomarkers for AKI.
Though SCr is the most widely used indicator of renal function, its use is associated with several 
disadvantages, like:
1.	 Non-renal metabolism: Creatinine also has significant GI excretion along with renal elimination, 
and in CKD this leads to overestimation of renal function.
2.	 Non-renal determinants: The SCr level is often influenced by multiple non-renal factors, like sex, 
age, body build, protein intake, exercise and concomitant drug therapy.
3.	 Slow in rise: It takes time to rise after the development of renal insult, delaying detection of renal 
dysfunction at an early stage and institution of necessary therapy.
17.	 What is the relation between CKD and ischaemic heart disease?
CKD is associated with cardiovascular (CV) mortality, which is independent of other risk factors 
like diabetes. CV mortality accounts for nearly half of the total mortality in advanced renal disease, 
while sudden cardiac death constitutes nearly two-thirds of CV mortality. The cause of increased 
sudden death is due to ischaemic heart disease, myocardial structural changes (hypertrophy, fibro-
sis), electrolyte imbalance and autonomic dysfunction.
Vascular changes occurring over time include atherosclerosis (with intimal calcium), arterioscle-
rosis and medial calcification. Calcification also causes accelerated coronary artery disease. Also, 
of importance are decreased compliance of the aorta and the resultant increase in cardiac afterload 
and ventricular hypertrophy. Cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk increases in both high and low 
(SBP <110 mmHg) blood pressure ranges. Thus, stiff arteries with higher pulse pressures have a 
higher risk of CVD.
In advanced renal disease due to inflammation (C-reactive protein [CRP] is raised in half of 
advanced disease cases) and malnutrition, increased mortality is paradoxically associated with 
lower cholesterol levels. Inflammation drives both the progression of CKD and atherosclerosis.
Mortality risk (especially sudden death) rises sharply when the phosphorus level increases 
above 6.5 mg/dL or when the calcium-phosphorus product increases beyond 72 mg2/dL2. Possible 
mechanisms include transformation of smooth muscle cells to osteoblast-like cells and progressive 
vascular calcification. Serum phosphorus levels in end-stage renal disease (ESRD) usually require 
treatment with dietary phosphorus restriction, adequate dialysis and the use of phosphate binders – 
calcium acetate and sevelamer.
The relation of anaemia with CV mortality is complex, and a haemoglobin target of 11gm/dL may 
be safer than higher levels.
18.	What are the imaging tests of choice in coronary artery disease in CKD?
Stress echocardiography, stress thallium and positron emission tomography (PET) perfusion scan 
may be useful. Echocardiography is the practical test at the bedside.
19.	 What are the salient points about acute coronary syndrome (ACS) management in CKD?
a.	 There are no formal dose adjustment recommendations for the use of streptokinase, alteplase, 
reteplase or tenecteplase in patients with CKD and ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI).
b.	 Mild to moderate CKD is considered a risk for major complications in patients with unstable 
angina or non-STEMI (NSTEMI), and an early invasive strategy is preferred to conservative 
medical management.
c.	 Patients with CKD who undergo angiography are at increased risk of CIN and AKI.
d.	 CKD patients have more extensive coronary atherosclerosis, which tends to be considerably 
more calcified; lesions tend to be more proximal and longer in length.
BK-TandF-SIKDAR_9781032455174-220973-Eresource_43.indd   5
29/03/23   3:09 PM
Sunandan Sikdar and Pinaki Mukhopadhyay
6
e.	 There are higher risks of bleeding and vascular complications. CKD patients had a higher fre-
quency of risk factors that predisposed them to a worse outcome, such as left main disease, vein 
graft or multivessel disease; complex, heavily calcified or ostial lesions; and ACS presentation.
f.	 Compared with PCI, coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) was associated with survival 
benefit in patients with severe CKD. PCI was associated with a survival benefit among patients 
with normal and mildly and moderately impaired renal function but not in patients with severe 
CKD Those with severe CKD and not on dialysis had the worst survival. Among patients with 
significant early renal dysfunction, treatment with PCI conferred better survival compared with 
CABG or medical therapy
g.	 Asymptomatic patients with CKD who have associated ischaemic heart disease (IHD) do 
not have a survival benefit by revascularization except in cases of triple vessel disease (3VD). 
However, asymptomatic 3VD is rare.
20.	What are the implications of renal transplant (RT) on IHD/CVD?
Post-transplant there is an increased risk of blood pressure and dyslipidaemia due to the use of 
steroids and cyclosporine. Obesity and hyperglycaemia are common. Similar to non-CKD, ste-
roids reduce cardiac mortality and non-fatal MI. Renal allograft dysfunction, proteinuria, anaemia, 
chronic inflammation, hyperhomocysteinemia, hypercoagulation and left ventricular hypertrophy 
(LVH) have all been linked to coronary artery risk after RT. Prolonged dialysis prior to RT also 
causes atherosclerosis progression. The presence of LV systolic dysfunction is a risk predictor.

44  Cardiac Drugs
Uses and Precautions
Sunandan Sikdar and Rana Rathore Roy
44.1  ANTICOAGULANTS
Heparin: Probably the most commonly used parenteral cardiac drug in the cardiac care unit (CCU), 
heparin has a narrow therapeutic window. It is isolated from porcine intestinal mucosa. Heparin 
consists of a sulphated polysaccharide which contains the unique pentasaccharide sequence that 
binds to antithrombin and augments its anticoagulant activity (Figure 44.1).
Pharmacokinetics and dosage: Better given in intravenous form due to its unpredictable subcutaneous 
absorption, it has a half-life of 30 min and has renal excretion. Activated partial thromboplastin 
time (aPTT) in the CCU and activated clotting time (ACT) in percutaneous coronary intervention/
coronary artery bypass grafting (PCI/CABG) (higher dosage of heparin) are the tests commonly 
used to monitor heparin. When intravenous heparin is used, aPTT should be 50–75 sec, correspond-
ing to 1.5–2 times the upper limit of normal. For coronary indications, the dosage is 60 U/kg (max 
4000 U) followed by continuous infusion of 12 U/kg (max 1000 U/hr); for venous thromboembolism 
(VTE) it is an intravenous bolus of 80 units/kg, followed by a continuous infusion at 18 units/kg/hr. 
In the PCI dosage without GP IIb/IIIa, it is 100U/kg (ACT 250–350 sec), while with GP IIb/IIIa, it is 
50 U/kg (ACT 200–250 sec). Intravenous heparin should not be given for more than 48 hr.
◾
◾If aPTT is three times control, reduce the dose by 50%; if 2–3, then reduce by 25%.
◾
◾If aPTT <1.5 times control, increase by 25%.
Side effects: Bleeding is the most common side effect. A higher aPTT increases cerebral bleeding 
without a survival advantage. Heparin should be avoided in endocarditis, bleeding disorders like 
haemophilia and liver disease/actively bleeding GI ulcer. It can be reversed by intravenous prot-
amine sulphate (contraindicated in salmon allergy) slowly, 50 mg (5 mL of 1% solution) given over 
10 min. Available as a 1% (10 mg/mL) solution of protamine sulphate, this drug itself possess am 
anticoagulant effect at high doses, and 10 mg protamine is required to neutralize 1000 units of 
heparin given in the previous 15 min. For earlier administration, the dose requirement of protamine 
comes down. Hypersensitivity is a serious side effect of protamine. Rapid IV administration causes 
pulmonary vasoconstriction, decreased left atrial pressure and hypotension, which often responds 
to fluid administration.
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) is an IgG-mediated syndrome of platelet destruction 
and paradoxical thrombosis (due to simultaneous platelet activation) which occurs in 3%–5% after 
unfractionated heparin (UFH) is given for 5 days or more (onset at 5–10 days). It is diagnosed clini-
cally by the four Ts: Thrombocytopenia (>50% drop in platelet count), Timing (5 days after starting 
heparin), Thrombosis and oTher causes ruled out. Confirmation of diagnosis is by serotonin release 
assay (SRA, sensitivity and specificity ~95%, gold standard but may not be available) and detec-
tion of platelet factor 4 antibodies by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay/Clinical Laboratory 
Improvement Amendments (ELISA/CLIA; sensitive, not specific but may be available). Atypical forms

paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (better than other antiarrhythmic drugs) and (4) atrial fibrillation car-
dioversion. Due to a lack of negative inotropic effects, it is used in borderline blood pressure to 
control the rate in atrial fibrillation (AFib)/atrial tachycardias. Rarely it has been used for supraven-
tricular tachycardia (SVT) with Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome, though these patients are 
usually best treated by ablation.
Pharmacokinetics: Each molecule of amiodarone contains two iodine atoms and is approximately 
37% of iodine by weight. The most commonly used oral dose of 200 mg/day results in an iodine 
uptake of 70 mg/day. About 10% (7 mg) is released in the body as iodine, which is an overwhelming 
amount compared to the normal daily iodine intake of 150–200 mcg.
After oral intake, only about 30%–50% is absorbed and is metabolized in the liver to produce the 
active metabolite desethylamiodarone. Due to its lipophilic nature, it has a large volume of distribution 
and high concentrations are found in fatty tissue, liver and lung. Steady-state concentration is reached 
only after 2 months. Serum concentrations >2.5 mg/L are associated with an increased risk of toxicity. 
The elimination half-life after oral long-term treatment is 50–60 days. High initial loading doses (about 
200 mg thrice daily for 1–2 weeks) may be necessary due to the large volume of distribution. The lowest 
effective oral dose is usually used (about 200 mg) because amiodarone has multiple side effects.
Intravenous amiodarone (bioavailability 100%) achieves peak concentration about 15 min after 
injection, but after rapid distribution to tissues there is a 10% fall in levels after about 30–45 min. 
Less of the active metabolite desethylamiodarone is produced. Intravenous amiodarone inhibits 
inactivated sodium channels, especially during shorter cycle lengths (use dependence) and more in 
ischaemic tissue and thus prevents ventricular tachycardia/ventricular fibrillation (VT/VF). Early 
on it has strong antiadrenergic effects. Further, amiodarone depresses sinus node automaticity, 
leading to bradycardia. However, the intravenous form causes peripheral vasodilation that leads 
sometimes to hypotension and reflex activation of the sympathetic system, which partially counters 
the degree of bradycardia. Though both oral and intravenous forms slow the nodal conduction, 
class III actions of the drug require time.
Intravenously, a bolus of 150 mg is usually administered over 10 min (may be prolonged to 
30–40 min in borderline haemodynamics), followed by a continuous infusion of 1200 mg/24 hr (a 
commonly used regimen in CCU is 60 mg/hr for 6 hours followed by 30 mg/hr for 18 hrs, bringing 
the total dose to 900 mg). If needed, a repeat 150-mg bolus can be given, though it may be preferable 
to add a beta-blocker in such cases.
Multiple drug interactions occur with amiodarone. It potentiates the effect of Coumadin deriva-
tives, and hence the dose of latter must be reduced by half. Similarly, the dose of digoxin should be 
reduced, as not only is the drug level increased, but the bradycardic effect is also potentiated. Though 
among the QT-prolonging antiarrhythmics, amiodarone is the safest, an additive proarrhythmic 
effect occurs with other drugs that prolong the QT interval, such as class IA antiarrhythmic drugs, 
tricyclic antidepressants, erythromycin, thiazide diuretics and sotalol. The risk of torsades also 
increases with hypokalaemia-causing agents such as diuretics and systemic steroids. Amiodarone 
also increases the levels of statins, calcium channel blockers (CCBs), fentanyl and flecainide.
While bradycardia and torsades (rare) are the cardiac side effects, the extracardiac side effects of 
amiodarone are legion and are given in Table 44.2.

  2.	What tests are needed to monitor amiodarone?
Thyroid profile: Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), T3, T4 and anti-TPO antibody, liver function

Flecainide: Pharmacodynamics – Originally developed for an anaesthetic use, it is a potent Na chan-
nel blocker with slow onset and offset kinetics belonging to the class Ic antiarrhythmic group. 
Prolongation of action potential duration (APD) in ventricular cells leads to QRS prolongation even 
at resting heart rates. In spite of potassium channel (I kr) blockage and QT prolongation, torsades is 
rare. At faster heart rates, the atrial APD is prolonged disproportionately, and this contributes to its 
efficacy in AFib. Thus, this drug causes PR, QRS and QT prolongation at rest.
Indications: It is used in pharmacological cardioversion (both oral and intravenous can be used) 
and rhythm control in AFib and prevention of recurrences. When used in prevention of recurrences, 
there is around 65% long-term response and about 50% short-term response. Two other niche indi-
cations of flecainide are unmasking of Brugada syndrome in patients with suspicious ECGs and

treating beta-blocker–refractory cases of catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia 
(CPVT). When used appropriately, it is a safe drug, and it has been used in cases of WPW syndrome 
with occasional AFib, as it slows down both the AV node and pathway conduction.
Pharmacokinetics: Flecainide is eliminated by renal excretion of the unchanged drug and hepatic 
metabolism (by CYP 2D6) of inactive metabolites. In renal dysfunction and with concomitant 
administration of cytochrome inhibitors, flecainide can accumulate to toxic levels.
QRS, PR and QT should be routinely monitored on patients initiated on flecainide. Toxicity (drug 
level in serum >1 mcg/mL) is suggested by a 50% increase in QRS duration (to 180 ms), 30% pro-
longation of the PR interval (to 260 ms) and/or 15% increase in the QTc interval. When these signs 
occur, flecainide should be discontinued because they reflect a substantial increase in the risk of 
both ventricular tachyarrhythmias and severe bradyarrhythmia.
Side effects: Dose-related blurred vision is the most common non-cardiac adverse effect. Transient 
asystole post-AFib termination and bradycardia are not uncommon. In patients with LV dysfunc-
tion flecainide can cause heart failure. In cases of atrial flutter flecainide may turn 2:1 conduction 
into 1:1 AV conduction and speed up the ventricular rate and cause haemodynamic compromise. 
Flecainide toxicity may also be manifested by neurologic effects, including sedation, confusion, 
paresthesias, ataxia, seizures and coma.
Contraindications to the drug include structural heart disease/LV dysfunction; second- or third-
degree atrioventricular block and bifascicular block without a pacemaker and non-sustained VT. It 
should be used with caution in post-infarction patients and those with hepatic or renal impairment.
Once flecainide toxicity is suspected, the following can be considered: Gastric lavage/activated 
charcoal if poisoning suspected (ingestion <1 hr), sodium bicarbonate infusion, intravenous fat 
emulsion (sequesters the drug) and lastly extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO).
Dosage: Oral – Start at 50 mg twice daily then increase over weeks to 100 mg twice daily. Rarely 
200 mg twice daily may be required (use caution). In intravenous form (uncommon) 1–2 mg/kg over 
10 min then 0.15–0.25 mg/kg/hr.
Lidocaine: Pharmacodynamics and indications – Lidocaine is a prototypical type 1 B antiarrhythmic 
which blocks both open and inactivated cardiac Na channels and is especially effective in isch-
aemia-related VT. It also reduces automaticity by reducing the slope of phase 4 depolarization and 
tissue excitability. It is one of the few antiarrhythmics that do not prolong PR, QRS and QT duration 
and has no haemodynamic ill effects.
Pharmacokinetics: Because of extensive first-pass metabolism, intravenous/intramuscular admin-
istration is required. On IV administration, it has biexponential reduction of plasma concentration, 
the first due to peripheral redistribution and the second due to hepatic metabolism (t½ 2 hr) by 
CYP3A4 enzymes into xylidine metabolites, one of which competes with the parent drug for the 
Na channel and reduces its efficacy after some time. Lidocaine reaches its steady state in 8–10 hr. If 
the loading dose of lidocaine controls the arrhythmia, maintenance infusion will provide benefit; 
otherwise, some other drug must be tried.
Dosage: Loading doses commonly used include 75–100 mg followed by another 50-mg dose 10 min 
later. The maintenance infusion is 2–4 mg/min (average 3 mg/min). The dose should be reduced in 
heart failure (volume of distribution low), the elderly and those with liver disease or those receiving 
propranolol (decreased metabolism).
Side effects: High bolus doses may precipitate seizures and central nervous system (CNS) side 
effects. This is even more true in cases where a brain injury occurs during VF or a cardiac arrest 
survivor is being treated with lidocaine. Bradyarrhythmia may also occur.
Phenytoin: Phenytoin is a class IB antiarrhythmic drug with a long half-life (t1/2 24 hr). The phar-
macokinetic characteristics of phenytoin are influenced markedly by its binding to serum proteins, 
by the nonlinearity of elimination kinetics (at increased concentrations, the elimination is increased 
out of proportion) and by its metabolism by the hepatic cytochrome oxidase system (CYP2C9 and, 
to a lesser extent, CYP2C19). The addition of warfarin can cause increased bleeding. Phenytoin is 
extensively bound (~90%) to serum proteins, mainly albumin. Small variations in the percentage of 
phenytoin that is bound dramatically affect the absolute amount of free (active) drug.
In cases of digitalis toxicity, atrial and ventricular tachyarrhythmias and in refractory ventricular 
arrhythmias, phenytoin has a useful role.

Its side effects include hypotension, vertigo, dysarthria, lethargy, gingivitis, macrocytic anae-
mia, hyperglycaemia and glucosuria, lupus and pulmonary infiltrates. Being an enzyme inducer, it 
reduces the level of many drugs. Co-administration of phenytoin and ticagrelor can reduce the drug 
level of the latter and cause increased ischaemic events. Cardiac toxicity occurs more frequently in 
the elderly and in those with known cardiac disease; it also can develop in young, healthy patients. 
Because of the risk of adverse cardiovascular reactions with rapid administration, IV administra-
tion should not exceed 50 mg/min in adults.
Ibutilide: Pharmacodynamics – Ibutilide, which has structural similarity to sotalol, is an inward 
potassium current (I kr) blocker and prolongs APD even at high heart rates. It causes dose-related 
prolongation of QT but not PR or QRS.
Pharmacokinetics: Due to extensive first-pass metabolism the intravenous formulation is used, and 
the drug is metabolized by CYP3A4/2D6 in the liver and excreted by the kidney. Requires caution 
in liver disease.
Dosage: Administered as 1 mg over a 10-min infusion. If AFib/atrial flutter persist after 10 min, 
then another infusion at the same specification is repeated. If body weight <60 kg, reduce the dose 
by 0.01 mg/kg. The infusion is stopped prematurely if sinus rhythm is restored or marked QT pro-
longation or torsades occurs.
Indication: Though useful in both, it is more effective in atrial flutter than in AFib. It increases the 
effectivity where cardioversion alone fails to terminate AFib. It can be used in cases under chronic 
amiodarone therapy. It is also useful in pre-excited AFib as it blocks antegrade pathway conduction 
and terminates AFib in parallel.
Side effects: Torsades is the side effect (3%–8%) to watch for at least 4 hr (drug t½ 6 hr), and this 
drug should be given in a CCU facility with resuscitation equipment.
Beta-blockers: Beta receptors act via G protein-coupled adenylate cyclase activation leading to 
phosphorylation of the calcium channel and promoting Ca entry (Figure 44.3). This leads to a pos-
itive inotropic and lusitropic (relaxant) effect. They are key drugs in chronic heart failure, IHD 
(especially acute coronary syndrome and post-infarct state), supraventricular and ventricular tachy-
cardias, long QT syndrome, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, hypertension, hyperthyroid states (espe-
cially propranolol), postural orthostatic tachycardia and aortic dissection (and also in associated 
conditions like Marfan syndrome or bicuspid aortic valve). Non-cardiac use includes glaucoma, 
migraine, anxiety and essential tremor. Beta blockade reduces fatty acid consumption and enhances 
usage of oxygen-conserving glucose as fuel, thus improving myocardial energetics. This effect of 
inhibiting lipolysis may cause weight gain during chronic use. Classifications include the following:
a.	 Nonselective: Propranolol, sotalol
b.	 Cardioselective: Atenolol, bisoprolol, metoprolol
c.	 Vasodilatory non-selective: Labetalol, carvedilol
d.	 Vasodilatory selective: Nebivolol

Side effects: Bronchospasm, bradycardia, depression, new-onset diabetes, fatigue, erectile dysfunction 
(use nebivolol to avoid this side effect) and weight gain. Propranolol (lipid soluble and crosses the blood-
brain barrier) can cause vivid dreams – this effect can be minimized by avoiding this drug at night.
Contraindications: Severe obstructive airway disease (use diltiazem), bradycardia/AV block, severe 
depression and severe peripheral vascular disease/gangrene.
◾
◾Atenolol: The first cardioselective beta-blocker. Its effectiveness as an antihypertensive agent is 
mitigated by a lack of improvement in outcomes.
◾
◾Metoprolol: This is the prototype cardioselective beta-blocker with an extended-release formula-
tion. It is extensively used in IHD and heart failure. Metoprolol is metabolized by cytochrome 
P450 and has significant genetic variation in its effects.
◾
◾Carvedilol: It is a non-selective alpha- and beta-blocker with extra benefits: Vasodilation, improve-
ment in insulin sensitivity and antioxidant effects. It is used for heart failure with LV dysfunction, for 
hypertension and for a post-MI state. Carvedilol is a beta blocker with most evidence base in Chronic 
Kidney Disease with heart failure and left ventricular dysfunction, even in those undergoing dialysis.
◾
◾Bisoprolol: Highly selective beta-blocker with use in IHD, hypertension and heart failure. It is 
highly protein bound, with a dosage to be reduced in hypoproteinaemia.
◾
◾Nebivolol: Highly selective beta-blocker with vasodilatory action and improvement of insulin sensi-
tivity. It is useful as an effective antihypertensive. The SENIORS trial established it as an anti-heart 
failure agent in the elderly population (especially those with LV ejection fraction [LVEF] <35%).
◾
◾Sotalol: It is a non-selective beta-blocker with a class III antiarrhythmic effect. It is useful in the 
maintenance of sinus rhythm in paroxysmal AFib and VT when the patient is already on an auto-
matic implantable cardiac defibrillator (AICD) and amiodarone cannot be used. Sotalol reduces 
the defibrillation threshold. A specific side effect is QT prolongation.
◾
◾Labetalol: It is a combined alpha- and beta-blocker useful in hypertensive crisis and in pregnancy-
induced hypertension.
Calcium Channel Blocker (CCBs): CCBs bind the alpha-one subunit of L-type calcium channels 
in the open state (Figure 44.4) with separate binding sites for each of the prototypes: Nifedipine, 
verapamil and diltiazem. While dihydropyridine CCBs (nifedipine and amlodipine or the more 
selective felodipine) are selective for peripheral vessels, nondihydropyridine CCBs (verapamil and 
diltiazem) are selective for the sinoatrial (SA) and AV nodes and reduce heart rate. While vera-
pamil and diltiazem reduce contractility, the same effect of dihydropyridine is counterbalanced by 
peripheral vasodilation-induced reflex sympathetic overactivity.
Dihydropyridine (DHP): One of the best drugs for control of hypertension and reduction of cardiac 
events, especially stroke, dihydropyridines are grouped into the following generations:

◾

Amlodipine: Due to its slow association and dissociation from the receptor, its slow onset and prolonged 
action are key advantages of the drug. Peak blood levels are reached after 6–12 hr, followed by extensive 
hepatic metabolism to inactive metabolites. The plasma levels increase during the chronic dosage. The 
elimination half-life is 35–48 hr. A common starting dose is 5 mg daily going up to 10 mg.
Verapamil and diltiazem: Both are nondihydropyridine CCBs which have multiple effects: (1) Anti-
ischaemic effect caused by the heart rate and contractility lowering action and increased collateral 
flow to the ischaemic area – useful in oral therapy in chronic stable angina with obstructive airway dis-
ease (beta-blocker contraindicated); (2) antiarrhythmic effect in lowering heart rate, useful in node-
dependent SVT for maintenance oral therapy. This effect is more prominent when the channel is more 
in an open state (frequency dependence); and (3) due to the negative inotropic effect both of these 
agents should be avoided in LV dysfunction so that heart failure is not precipitated. This aspect of 
verapamil’s effect is useful in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy where it controls symptoms at rest.
The other side effect common to both is bradycardia. Both of these drugs should be avoided in WPW 
syndrome with AFib, as they can accelerate the heart rate by selective AV node block. Constipation 
is common with all CCBs, especially verapamil. The verapamil level increases in liver and renal 
disease. Hepatic interactions of verapamil include inhibition of CYP3A4, thus decreasing the break-
down of atorvastatin and simvastatin while digoxin levels are increased. Diltiazem has less interac-
tion in the case of concurrent administration with digoxin and is therefore preferred where both a 
CCB and digoxin is needed for rate control. While verapamil has predominantly renal excretion, dil-
tiazem is less so. Other drug interactions where caution is required while using verapamil include 
inducers like phenytoin, rifampicin (decreased verapamil efficacy), theophylline, carbamazepine 
(increased blood levels of these drugs), sildenafil and lithium. Both of these drugs are used pre-
dominantly for oral therapy in the current era.
◾
◾Oral dose of verapamil: 180–480 mg daily in two or three doses (titrated). For the elderly/those with 
borderline BP/frail: 40 mg thrice daily (120 mg) suffices.
◾
◾Oral dose of diltiazem: 120–360 mg daily in three or four doses. For the frail/elderly 30 mg thrice 
daily or controlled delivery (CD) (90 mg) once daily will suffice.
Sustained/controlled-release preparations of both drugs, given once daily, are available on the 
market.
Ivabradine: Ivabradine selectively blocks the intracellular aspect of the Hyperpolarisation activated 
Cyclic Nucleotide gated ion channel (HCN) which is actually a Na-K channel (funny current) in the SA 
node (Figure 44.5). This leads to a reduction in the slope of diastolic depolarization and hence slows the 
heart rate. It blocks the channel in the open state, causing it to be more potent at a higher heart rate (use 
dependence). This dose-dependent effect occurs without hypotension or negative inotropy.

The dose of ivabradine is 2.5 mg or 5 mg twice daily. It achieves peak concentration by 1 hr in 
the fasting state (food delays its action by 1 hr). It undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism in the 
liver by the cytochrome enzyme CYP3A4. The principal cardiac side effect of ivabradine is brady-
cardia. It is contraindicated in patients with sick sinus syndrome and relatively contraindicated in 
patients with AV block and should be used with caution in first-degree AV block. It can be used 
in pacemaker patients to reduce the ventricular pacing in those patients who have atrial-sensed–
ventricular-paced beats. It causes an increase in relative risk in AFib by 15% and predisposes to 
torsades. It should be avoided with QT-prolonging drugs. The most common non-cardiac side effect 
is transient brightness in the visual field called phosphenes. It caused by the effect of the drug on the 
hyperpolarization-activated (Ih) current within the retina. It also has a teratogenic effect.
Principal uses for ivabradine are stable patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction 
(HFrEF) (LVEF ≤35%) and a heart rate of ≥70 bpm on maximally tolerated beta-blockers or when 
beta-blockers are contraindicated (SHIFT trial), uncontrolled angina with heart rate>70 bpm despite 
optimal beta-blocker therapy or patients with intolerance/contraindications to them (BEAUTIFUL, 
SIGNIFY trials), in inappropriate sinus tachycardia (along with beta-blockers) and in selected cases 
of ectopic junctional tachycardia.
Adenosine: See the chapter on narrow QRS tachycardia.
44.3  ANTIANGINALS
Nicorandil: This is a balanced vasodilator that combines the KATP channel’s opening action on 
the arterial system and nitrate-like action on the venous system (using guanylate cyclase) and has 
been used for the treatment of angina pectoris (tablet formula) and unstable angina (injection for-
mula). In IHD, apart from afterload reduction, nicorandil improves the coronary circulation by 
dilating coronary resistance vessels in addition to large coronary arteries. Nicorandil also has a 
myocardial-protective effect from reperfusion injury following PCI procedures. It is used usually in 
the CCU as a continuous infusion @ 0.1 mg/kg/hr. In acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF), 
nicorandil has been used with a loading bolus dose of 0.2 mg/kg/5 min followed by an infusion 
@ 0.2 mg/kg/hr with improvement in haemodynamics (improves cardiac index [CI] and reduces 
pulmonary capillary wedge pressure [PCWP]). Nicorandil can reduce preload in lower infusion 
rates of 0.05–0.10 mg/kg/hr, but for further improvement in the afterload and CI, a higher infu-
sion rate of 0.20 mg/kg/hr would be more appropriate. A bolus dose of nicorandil reduces systolic 
blood pressure, but in maintenance doses, low to normal systolic blood pressures are not affected. 
However, there is a significant decrease of high systolic blood pressure. Diastolic blood pressure is 
reduced across all ranges of systolic pressure due to vasodilation. Guidelines recommend only oral 
nicorandil as an added antianginal in chronic ischemic heart disease for symptom relief.
Statins: See the chapter on acute coronary syndrome.
44.4  OTHER DRUGS
See the chapter on heart failure for information on nitroglycerin (NTG), angiotensin-converting 
enzyme inhibitors (ACEIs), angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), angiotensin receptor/neprilysin 
inhibitors (ARNIs), spironolactone and loop diuretics.
See the chapter on refractory hypertension on for information on hydralazine, alpha methyl dopa, 
minoxidil and nitroprusside.
See the chapter on inotropes and vasopressors for information on noradrenaline, adrenaline, dobu-
tamine, dopamine, levosimendan and milrinone.
Addenda
The infusion rate of a drug (mL/hr) = dose (mcg/kg/min) × body wt in kg × 60/concentration of 
solution (mcg/mL).
